> **M1**: Using similar solids to obtain $a = 0 . 4 h$, or equivalently $h = 2 . 5 a$, with the units made consistent.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting to obtain $V$ in terms of $h$ only, and differentiating to reach $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = \frac{4h^{2}}{25}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} \times \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$.
> 
> **A1**: A correct expression for the rate, $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \frac{450}{h^{2}}$, or any equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: The correct rate, $\frac{1}{8}$ or $0 . 125$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A curve has equation $y = 5 - ( x - 3 )^{2}$.

$A$ is the point on the curve with $x$-coordinate 0, and $B$ is the point on the curve with $x$-coordinate 6.

$C$ is the point of intersection of the tangents to the curve at $A$ and $B$.

Find the coordinates of point $C$.
parts.solutionMd:
A tangent needs a point and a gradient, so start with the two points. Substitute each $x$-coordinate into the curve

$\text{At} A :   y = 5 - ( 0 - 3 )^{2} = - 4   \Rightarrow   A ( 0 , - 4 )$

$\text{At} B :   y = 5 - ( 6 - 3 )^{2} = - 4   \Rightarrow   B ( 6 , - 4 )$

**[M1 A1]**

The gradient of a tangent is given by the derivative. Expand the bracket first, so that the power rule applies term by term

`y = 5 - \left(x^{2} - 6x + 9\right) = -x^{2} + 6x - 4`

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 x + 6$

**[M1]**

Substitute $A$'s $x$-coordinate to get the gradient there, then form the straight line through $A$ with that gradient

$\text{At} A :   \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 ( 0 ) + 6 = 6$

$y - ( - 4 ) = 6 ( x - 0 )   \Rightarrow   y = 6 x - 4$

**[M1]**

Repeat at $B$

$\text{At} B :   \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 ( 6 ) + 6 = - 6$

$y - ( - 4 ) = - 6 ( x - 6 )   \Rightarrow   y = - 6 x + 32$

**[M1]**

$C$ lies on both tangents, so its coordinates satisfy both equations at once. Set the two right-hand sides equal

$6 x - 4 = - 6 x + 32$

$12 x = 36   \Rightarrow   x = 3$

**[M1]**

Substitute back into either tangent to get the matching $y$-coordinate

$y = 6 ( 3 ) - 4 = 14$

$C ( 3 , 14 )$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There is a shortcut worth full marks if you justify it. $A$ and $B$ have the same $y$-coordinate, so they sit symmetrically either side of the curve's axis of symmetry $x = 3$; the tangents at $A$ and $B$ are mirror images, and mirror images meet on the mirror line. That gives $x_{C} = \frac{0+6}{2} = 3$ straight away, without ever finding the tangent at $B$, and substituting into $y = 6 x - 4$ gives $y_{C} = 14$. You must write the reason, "by symmetry", rather than simply asserting $x = 3$. Even so, the simultaneous route above is the one to learn: it works for any two points on any curve, whereas this shortcut exists only because $5 - ( 0 - 3 )^{2}$ and $5 - ( 6 - 3 )^{2}$ happen to be equal.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $x = 0$ and $x = 6$ into the curve equation to find the $y$-coordinates of $A$ and $B$.
> 
> **A1**: Both points correct, $A ( 0 , - 4 )$ and $B ( 6 , - 4 )$.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiating to obtain $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 x + 6$, or the equivalent $- 2 ( x - 3 )$. Expanding the bracket first is the simplest way in.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $x = 0$ into your $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ and forming the equation of the tangent at $A$.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $x = 6$ into your $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ and forming the equation of the tangent at $B$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving your two tangent equations simultaneously.
> 
> **A1**: $C ( 3 , 14 )$.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the area of triangle $A B C$.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ and $B$ share the $y$-coordinate $- 4$, so $A B$ is horizontal. That makes it the natural base, and the height is then the vertical distance from $C$ down to it

![Sketch of the parabola y = 5 − (x − 3) squared with the tangents at A(0, −4) and B(6, −4) meeting at C(3, 14). A and B are joined by a horizontal dashed base, and a dashed vertical from C meets that base at a right angle, giving the height of triangle ABC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/002-sketch-of-the-parabola-y-5-x-3-squared-with-the-.png)

Read both lengths off as differences of coordinates

$\text{base} A B = 6 - 0 = 6$

$\text{height} = 14 - ( - 4 ) = 18$

**[M1]**

Apply the formula for the area of a triangle

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} ( 6 ) ( 18 )$

$\text{Area} = 54$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A complete method for the area, such as $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ with base $A B = 6$ and perpendicular height $14 - ( - 4 ) = 18$. Follow through on your coordinates from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: 54.

parts.problemMd:
A curve is described by the equation $y = \text{f} ( x )$, where

$\text{f} ( x ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} ,   x > 0$

$P$ is the point on the curve such that the normal to the curve at $P$ also passes through the origin.

Find the coordinates of point $P$. Give your answer in the form `\left(2^{a}, 2^{b}\right)`, where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
The power rule needs a power of $x$. A root is a power of $\frac{1}{2}$, and a root in a denominator makes that power negative

$\text{f} ( x ) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Differentiate, multiplying by the power and reducing it by 1

$\text{f} ' ( x ) = - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}-1} = - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$

**[M1 A1]**

Call the point `P\left(x_{P}, y_{P}\right)`. The tangent's gradient there is `\text{f}'\left(x_{P}\right)`, and a normal is perpendicular to its tangent, so invert that gradient and change its sign

`m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{1}{\text{f}'\left(x_{P}\right)} = -\dfrac{1}{-\frac{1}{2}x_{P}^{-\frac{3}{2}}} = 2x_{P}^{\frac{3}{2}}`

**[M1]**

The normal also passes through the origin, which gives a second way to write the same gradient: the rise over the run between $O ( 0 , 0 )$ and $P$

$m_{\text{normal}} = \frac{y_{P}-0}{x_{P}-0} = \frac{y_{P}}{x_{P}}$

Two expressions for one gradient must be equal, and that is what produces an equation to solve

$2 x_{P}^{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{y_{P}}{x_{P}}$

**[M1]**

$P$ lies on the curve, so its coordinates satisfy $y = \text{f} ( x )$. Replacing $y_{P}$ leaves $x_{P}$ as the only unknown

$2 x_{P}^{\frac{3}{2}} = \frac{x_{P}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}{x_{P}} = x_{P}^{-\frac{3}{2}}$

Divide both sides by $x_{P}^{\frac{3}{2}}$, subtracting the powers

$2 = x_{P}^{-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{3}{2}} = x_{P}^{-3}$

**[M1]**

A negative power is a reciprocal, so invert both sides and then take the cube root

`x_{P}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x_{P} = \left(2^{-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 2^{-\frac{1}{3}}`

Substitute back into the curve for the $y$-coordinate, multiplying the powers

`y_{P} = \left(2^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 2^{\frac{1}{6}}`

**Final answer:** `P\left(2^{-\frac{1}{3}}, \; 2^{\frac{1}{6}}\right)`**, so **$a = - \frac{1}{3}$** and **$b = \frac{1}{6}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Rewriting $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ as $x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ and differentiating, with the power reduced by 1.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{f} ' ( x ) = - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$, or any equivalent surd form.
> 
> **M1**: Using the perpendicular relationship to write the normal's gradient as `-\dfrac{1}{\text{f}'\left(x_{P}\right)}`, giving $2 x_{P}^{\frac{3}{2}}$.
> 
> **M1**: Using the fact that the normal passes through the origin to write its gradient as $\frac{y_{P}}{x_{P}}$, and equating the two expressions.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $y_{P} = x_{P}^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ and solving for $x_{P}$, reaching $x_{P}^{3} = \frac{1}{2}$ or $x_{P}^{-3} = 2$.
> 
> **A1**: `P\left(2^{-\frac{1}{3}}, 2^{\frac{1}{6}}\right)`, with $a = - \frac{1}{3}$ and $b = \frac{1}{6}$.

parts.problemMd: Write down the equation of the normal to the curve at $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
The normal passes through the origin, so it has no intercept and takes the form $y = m x$. Its gradient is the rise over the run from $O$ to $P$, and part (a) has already supplied both coordinates

`m = \dfrac{y_{P}}{x_{P}} = \dfrac{2^{\frac{1}{6}}}{2^{-\frac{1}{3}}} = 2^{\frac{1}{6}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)} = 2^{\frac{1}{2}}`

$y = \sqrt{2} x$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $y = \sqrt{2} x$, or the equivalent $y = 2^{\frac{1}{2}} x$.

parts.problemMd:
Show that an equation of the tangent to the curve at $P$ is

`\left(2^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)x + \left(2^{\frac{5}{6}}\right)y = 3`
parts.solutionMd:
The tangent and the normal at $P$ are perpendicular, so invert the normal's gradient from part (b) and change the sign

$m = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

**[M1]**

Form the straight line through $P$ with that gradient, taking the coordinates from part (a)

`y - 2^{\frac{1}{6}} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(x - 2^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)`

Expand the bracket. Writing $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ as $2^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ keeps every number a power of 2, so the indices can simply be added

$y - 2^{\frac{1}{6}} = - 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} x + 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} \times 2^{-\frac{1}{3}} = - 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} x + 2^{-\frac{5}{6}}$

**[M1]**

The target has no fractions and no negative powers. Look at the coefficient of $y$ that is being aimed for: multiplying through by $2^{\frac{5}{6}}$ clears everything in one step

$2^{\frac{5}{6}} y - 2^{\frac{5}{6}} \times 2^{\frac{1}{6}} = - 2^{\frac{5}{6}} \times 2^{-\frac{1}{2}} x + 2^{\frac{5}{6}} \times 2^{-\frac{5}{6}}$

**[M1]**

Add the indices in each product

$2^{\frac{5}{6}} y - 2^{1} = - 2^{\frac{1}{3}} x + 2^{0}$

$2^{\frac{5}{6}} y - 2 = - 2^{\frac{1}{3}} x + 1$

Collect the $x$ and $y$ terms on the left and the constants on the right

`\left(2^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)x + \left(2^{\frac{5}{6}}\right)y = 3`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using the perpendicular relationship to get the tangent's gradient from the normal's, $m = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ or $- 2^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Differentiating again to get `\text{f}'\left(2^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)` directly is equally acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Forming the equation of the tangent through $P$ with your gradient.
> 
> **M1**: Multiplying through to clear the fractional powers, by $2^{\frac{5}{6}}$ or by any combination that does the same job.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching `\left(2^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)x + \left(2^{\frac{5}{6}}\right)y = 3` with no errors. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the part of the curve with equation $y = 3 - \frac{1}{4} x^{2}$ for which $y > 0$. The marked point $P ( x , y )$ lies on the curve. $O$ is the origin.

![A curve rising to a peak on the y-axis and falling to meet the x-axis on either side, with only the part above the x-axis drawn. The origin is labelled O, and a point labelled P(x, y) is marked on the curve to the left of the y-axis.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/006-a-curve-rising-to-a-peak-on-the-y-axis-and-falli.png)

Show that $O P^{2} = 9 - \frac{1}{2} x^{2} + \frac{1}{16} x^{4}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Dropping a vertical from $P$ to the $x$-axis makes a right-angled triangle with $O$, whose horizontal side is $x$ and whose vertical side is $y$. Pythagoras then gives the square of the distance

$O P^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$

**[M1]**

The target is in terms of $x$ alone, and $P$ lies on the curve, so use its equation to replace $y$

`OP^{2} = x^{2} + \left(3 - \dfrac{1}{4}x^{2}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Expand the bracket, remembering the middle term of the square

$O P^{2} = x^{2} + 9 - \frac{3}{2} x^{2} + \frac{1}{16} x^{4}$

Collect the two $x^{2}$ terms

$O P^{2} = 9 - \frac{1}{2} x^{2} + \frac{1}{16} x^{4}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using Pythagoras or the distance formula to write $O P^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $y = 3 - \frac{1}{4} x^{2}$ to eliminate $y$.
> 
> **A1**: Expanding and simplifying to reach the given result with no errors. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Find the minimum distance from $O$ to the curve, using calculus to prove that your answer is indeed a minimum.
parts.solutionMd:
$O P$ is never negative, and squaring keeps quantities in the same order, so $O P$ is smallest exactly where $O P^{2}$ is smallest. That means part (a)'s quartic can be minimised instead of the square root, which is why it was worth forming

$O P^{2} = 9 - \frac{1}{2} x^{2} + \frac{1}{16} x^{4}$

Differentiate it with respect to $x$

`\dfrac{\text{d}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x} = -x + \dfrac{1}{4}x^{3}`

**[M1 A1]**

A minimum is a stationary point, so set the derivative to zero. Take out the common factor of $x$ rather than dividing by it, so that no solution is lost

`-x + \dfrac{1}{4}x^{3} = 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; x\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{4} - 1\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Each factor gives solutions

$x = 0$* or *$x^{2} = 4   \Rightarrow   x = \pm 2$

**[A1]**

There are three stationary points, so they must be told apart. Differentiate a second time

`\dfrac{\text{d}^{2}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x^{2}} = -1 + \dfrac{3}{4}x^{2}`

**[M1]**

Test each stationary value in turn

`\text{At } x = 0: \;\; \dfrac{\text{d}^{2}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x^{2}} = -1 < 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{maximum}`

`\text{At } x = \pm 2: \;\; \dfrac{\text{d}^{2}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x^{2}} = -1 + 3 = 2 > 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{minimum}`

**[A1]**

The curve is symmetric about the $y$-axis, so $x = 2$ and $x = - 2$ are mirror images and give the same distance. Substitute either into part (a)'s expression

$O P^{2} = 9 - \frac{1}{2} ( 2 )^{2} + \frac{1}{16} ( 2 )^{4} = 9 - 2 + 1 = 8$

**[M1]**

Take the square root to turn the squared distance back into a distance

$O P_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{8} = 2 \sqrt{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiating your $O P^{2}$ with respect to $x$.
> 
> **A1**: `\dfrac{\text{d}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x} = -x + \dfrac{1}{4}x^{3}`.
> 
> **M1**: Setting your derivative equal to zero and factorising, or otherwise solving.
> 
> **A1**: All three stationary values, $x = 0$ and $x = \pm 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Finding the second derivative, `\dfrac{\text{d}^{2}\left(OP^{2}\right)}{\text{d}x^{2}} = -1 + \dfrac{3}{4}x^{2}`, or using a valid sign test instead.
> 
> **A1**: Classifying correctly, with the substitution and the comparison to zero both shown: $x = 0$ gives a maximum and $x = \pm 2$ gives a minimum.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting your minimising value into $O P^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $O P_{\text{min}} = 2 \sqrt{2}$. Accept $\sqrt{8}$ or $2 . 83$.

parts.problemMd:
The top of a patio table is to be made in the shape of a sector of a circle with radius $r$ and central angle $θ$, where $θ$ is strictly between 0° and 360°.

![A sector of a circle with its vertex at the bottom, opening upwards. The two straight edges are each labelled r, and the angle between them at the vertex is labelled θ.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/005-a-sector-of-a-circle-with-its-vertex-at-the-bott.png)

Although $r$ and $θ$ may be varied, it is necessary that the table have a fixed area of $A \text{m}^{2}$.

Explain why $r > \sqrt{\frac{A}{π}}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The angle is strictly less than 360°, so the sector is only part of the circle it is cut from, never the whole of it. Its area is therefore strictly less than the area of that full circle

$A < π r^{2}$

**[M1]**

Divide by $π$, then take the square root. The radius is a length, so only the positive root applies and the direction of the inequality is unchanged

$r^{2} > \frac{A}{π}$

**Final answer:** $r > \sqrt{\frac{A}{π}}$**, since the sector's area **$A$** is fixed and must be less than **$π r^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Stating that the sector's area is less than that of the full circle, $A < π r^{2}$, or the equivalent $π r^{2} > A$.
> 
> **A1**: Rearranging correctly to $r > \sqrt{\frac{A}{π}}$, together with a clear reason. The reason is the mark: an unexplained rearrangement does not answer an "explain why" question.

parts.problemMd:
Show that the perimeter, $P$, of the table top is given by the formula

$P = 2 r + \frac{2A}{r}$
parts.solutionMd:
The perimeter runs along both straight edges and then round the curved arc. Each straight edge is a radius, and the arc is the fraction $\frac{θ}{360}$ of the full circumference

`P = 2r + 2\pi r\left(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\right)`

The target contains no $θ$, so it has to go. The fixed area gives a second equation linking $θ$ to $r$, since the sector is the same fraction of the circle's area

`A = \pi r^{2}\left(\dfrac{\theta}{360}\right) \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \theta = \dfrac{360A}{\pi r^{2}}`

**[M1]**

Substitute that into the perimeter. The $360$ and the $π$ both cancel, and one power of $r$ cancels with the $r^{2}$

$P = 2 r + \frac{2πr}{360} \times \frac{360A}{πr^{2}} = 2 r + \frac{2A}{r}$

$P = 2 r + \frac{2A}{r}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Writing the perimeter as two radii plus the arc, and using the fixed area to get $θ$ in terms of $A$ and $r$.
> 
> **A1**: Substituting and simplifying to the given result with no errors. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd: Show that the minimum possible value for $P$ is equal to the perimeter of a square with area $A$. Be sure to prove that your value is a minimum.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ is fixed, so $P$ depends on $r$ alone. Write the fraction as a negative power so the power rule applies, then differentiate with respect to $r$

$P = 2 r + 2 A r^{-1}$

$\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}r} = 2 - 2 A r^{-2}$

**[M1 A1]**

The minimum is a stationary point, so set the derivative to zero

$2 - \frac{2A}{r^{2}} = 0   \Rightarrow   r^{2} = A$

The radius is positive, so take the positive root

$r = \sqrt{A}$

**[M1]**

The question insists on a proof, so differentiate a second time and check the sign at that radius

$\frac{\text{d}^{2}P}{\text{d}r^{2}} = 4 A r^{-3} = \frac{4A}{r^{3}}$

Both $A$ and $r$ are positive, so this is positive for every permitted radius, and the stationary point is therefore a minimum

`\dfrac{\text{d}^{2}P}{\text{d}r^{2}} = 4A\left(\sqrt{A}\right)^{-3} = 4A^{-\frac{1}{2}} > 0 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{minimum}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the minimising radius back into the perimeter. The second term simplifies because $\frac{2A}{\sqrt{A}} = 2 \sqrt{A}$

$P_{\text{min}} = 2 \sqrt{A} + \frac{2A}{\sqrt{A}} = 2 \sqrt{A} + 2 \sqrt{A} = 4 \sqrt{A}$

A square of area $A$ has side $\sqrt{A}$, so its perimeter is four of those sides

$P_{\text{square}} = 4 \times \sqrt{A} = 4 \sqrt{A}$

$P_{\text{min}} = P_{\text{square}} = 4 \sqrt{A}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiating your $P$ with respect to $r$, treating $A$ as a constant.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{\text{d}P}{\text{d}r} = 2 - 2 A r^{-2}$, or any equivalent such as $2 - \frac{2A}{r^{2}}$.
> 
> **M1**: Setting your derivative to zero and solving to obtain $r = \sqrt{A}$.
> 
> **M1**: Using the second derivative and stating its sign to prove a minimum, or using a valid sign test instead.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching $P_{\text{min}} = 4 \sqrt{A}$ and identifying it as the perimeter of a square of side $\sqrt{A}$. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
An expanding spherical air bubble has radius $r$ cm at time $t$ seconds, determined by the function

$r ( t ) = 0 . 3 + 0 . 1 t^{2}$

The bubble will burst if the rate of expansion of its volume exceeds $4 t \text{cm}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$.

Find, to one decimal place, the length of time the bubble expands for.
parts.solutionMd:
The radius is given directly as a function of time, so its rate of change comes straight from differentiating it

$\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = 0 . 2 t$

**[M1]**

The bubble is a sphere, and its volume depends on the radius

$V = \frac{4}{3} π r^{3}   \Rightarrow   \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}r} = 4 π r^{2}$

**[M1]**

The chain rule links the volume's rate of expansion to the two rates now known

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}r} \times \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = 4 π r^{2} \times 0 . 2 t$

**[M1]**

The bubble bursts at the instant this expansion rate reaches the given threshold, so set the two equal and replace $r$ by its formula

`4\pi\left(0.3 + 0.1t^{2}\right)^{2}\left(0.2t\right) = 4t`

Both sides carry a factor of $t$. The bubble is expanding, so $t > 0$ and dividing by $t$ is safe. That leaves no $t$ outside the bracket at all

`0.8\pi\left(0.3 + 0.1t^{2}\right)^{2} = 4 \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \left(0.3 + 0.1t^{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{5}{\pi}`

**[M1]**

Expand the bracket, then multiply through by 100 to clear the decimals

$0 . 09 + 0 . 06 t^{2} + 0 . 01 t^{4} = \frac{5}{π}$

$t^{4} + 6 t^{2} + 9 = \frac{500}{π}$

The left-hand side is a perfect square, which avoids having to treat this as a quadratic in $t^{2}$

`\left(t^{2} + 3\right)^{2} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}`

**[A1]**

Take the square root. Only the positive root is worth taking, since $t^{2} + 3$ is positive

$t^{2} = \sqrt{\frac{500}{π}} - 3 = 9 . 6156 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 3 . 1 \text{s}$** (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiating the given radius function to obtain $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} = 0 . 2 t$.
> 
> **M1**: Using the volume of a sphere and differentiating, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}r} = 4 π r^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}r} \times \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$.
> 
> **M1**: Setting your $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ equal to $4 t$, substituting for $r$, and cancelling the $t$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching a correct solvable equation, such as `\left(0.3 + 0.1t^{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{5}{\pi}` or `\left(t^{2}+3\right)^{2} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}`.
> 
> **A1**: $t = 3 . 1$. Accept answers which round to $3 . 1$.

parts.problemMd:
A small conical pot, stood on its base, is being filled with salt via a small hole at its vertex. The cone has a height of 6 cm and a radius of 2 cm.

Salt is being poured into the pot at a constant rate of $0 . 3 \text{cm}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$.

Find, to three significant figures, the rate of change in depth of the salt at the instant when the pot is half full by volume.
parts.solutionMd:
![Diagram of the conical pot standing on its base, with the wide circular base of radius 2 cm at the bottom and the vertex at the top; the full height 6 cm is shown by a bracket on the right. A dashed ellipse partway up marks the salt surface, of radius r, with the salt depth h shown by a bracket on the left and the empty cone above it, of height 6 minus h, shown by a shorter bracket on the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/004-diagram-of-the-conical-pot-standing-on-its-base-.png)

The rate given is a volume per unit time, and the pot is filling, so it is positive

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = 0 . 3$

Find the volume of the full pot

$V_{\text{pot}} = \frac{1}{3} π ( 2 )^{2} ( 6 ) = 8 π$

**[M1]**

The pot stands on its base, so its vertex points upwards and the salt fills the wide end first. The salt is therefore not a cone, and has no formula of its own. What *is* a cone is the empty gap above it, of height $6 - h$ and radius $r$, and that gap is similar to the whole pot

$\frac{6}{2} = \frac{6-h}{r}   \Rightarrow   r = \frac{1}{3} ( 6 - h )$

**[M1]**

So the salt's volume is the whole pot with that empty cone taken away

`V = 8\pi - \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left[\dfrac{1}{3}(6-h)\right]^{2}(6 - h) = 8\pi - \dfrac{\pi}{27}(6 - h)^{3}`

**[M1]**

Differentiate with respect to the depth

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = \frac{π}{9} ( 6 - h )^{2}$

**[A1]**

The chain rule links the rate wanted to the two rates now known

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} \times \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}   \Rightarrow   0 . 3 = \frac{π}{9} ( 6 - h )^{2} \times \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$

$\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \frac{27}{10π(6-h)^{2}}$

**[M1]**

The instant is given by volume, not depth, so the depth has to be found first. Half full means half of $8 π$

$4 π = 8 π - \frac{π}{27} ( 6 - h )^{3}   \Rightarrow   ( 6 - h )^{3} = 108$

Take the cube root rather than expanding the bracket

`6 - h = \sqrt[3]{108} = 4.7622\ldots`

**[M1]**

Substitute that straight into the rate, keeping it unrounded

`\dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{27}{10\pi\left(4.7622\ldots\right)^{2}}`

**Final answer:** $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = 0 . 0379 \text{cm s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = 0 . 3$ and finding the pot's total volume, $8 π$.
> 
> **M1**: Using similar triangles on the empty cone above the salt to obtain $r = \frac{1}{3} ( 6 - h )$.
> 
> **M1**: Forming the salt's volume by subtraction, $V = 8 π - \frac{π}{27} ( 6 - h )^{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = \frac{π}{9} ( 6 - h )^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} \times \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$.
> 
> **M1**: Using "half full by volume" to set $V = 4 π$ and solving for the depth, $h = 1 . 24$ or $6 - h = 4 . 76$.
> 
> **A1**: $0 . 0379$. Accept answers which round to $0 . 0379$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A large block of ice used by sculptors is in the shape of a cuboid with dimensions $x$ m by $2 x$ m by $5 x$ m. The block melts uniformly, with its surface area decreasing at a constant rate of $k$$\text{m}^{2} \text{s}^{-1}$. You may assume that as the block melts, the shape remains mathematically similar to the original cuboid.

Show that the rate of melting, by volume, is given by

$\frac{15kx}{34} \text{m}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$
parts.solutionMd:
![Diagram of the cuboid block of ice drawn in 3D as a long rectangular bar. The small front face is 2x wide and x tall, and the block extends 5x back into the depth; the three edge lengths are labelled x, 2x and 5x.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/003-diagram-of-the-cuboid-block-of-ice-drawn-in-3d-a.png)

The block stays mathematically similar as it melts, so the sides keep the ratio $1 : 2 : 5$ and the single variable $x$ describes the whole solid. The surface area is falling, so its rate is negative

$\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} = - k$

**[M1]**

Write the volume in terms of $x$ and differentiate

$V = x ( 2 x ) ( 5 x ) = 10 x^{3}   \Rightarrow   \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}x} = 30 x^{2}$

**[M1]**

A cuboid has three pairs of identical faces, so add the three distinct face areas and double

`A = 2\left(2x^{2} + 5x^{2} + 10x^{2}\right) = 34x^{2} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \dfrac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}x} = 68x`

**[M1]**

There is no direct link between the area's rate and the volume's rate, so $x$ has to bridge them. That needs three factors rather than the usual two, and the middle one is a reciprocal

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}x} \times \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}A} \times \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$*, where *$\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}A} = \frac{1}{68x}$

**[M1]**

Substitute all three

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = 30 x^{2} \times \frac{1}{68x} \times ( - k ) = - \frac{30kx}{68} = - \frac{15kx}{34}$

The negative sign says the volume is falling. The rate of *melting* is how fast that volume is lost, which is a positive quantity, so it is the size of this rate

$\text{rate of melting} = \frac{15kx}{34} \text{m}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising that the area is decreasing, so $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} = - k$.
> 
> **M1**: $V = 10 x^{3}$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}x} = 30 x^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: $A = 34 x^{2}$ and $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}x} = 68 x$.
> 
> **M1**: A correct chain linking the three rates, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}x} \times \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}A} \times \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$, with $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}A}$ used as the reciprocal of $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}x}$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching $\frac{15kx}{34}$, with the negative sign correctly accounted for. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
In the case when $k = 0 . 2$, the block of ice remains solid enough to be sculpted as long as the rate of melting, by volume, does not exceed $0 . 05 \text{m}^{3} \text{s}^{-1}$.

Find the value of $x$ for the largest block of ice that can be used for ice sculpting under such conditions, giving your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate of melting grows with $x$, so the biggest usable block is the one sitting exactly on the limit. Take the expression from part (a) and put it at the threshold

$\frac{15(0.2)x}{34} = 0 . 05$

**[M1]**

Simplify the left-hand side, then multiply out

$\frac{3x}{34} = 0 . 05   \Rightarrow   3 x = 34 \times 0 . 05 = 1 . 7$

$x = \frac{1.7}{3} = \frac{34}{60}$

**[M1]**

Cancel the common factor of 2 to put the fraction in its lowest terms

$x = \frac{17}{30}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $k = 0 . 2$ into your part (a) expression and setting it against $0 . 05$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving for $x$, reaching $\frac{34}{60}$, $\frac{1.7}{3}$ or any correct unsimplified equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \frac{17}{30}$. The fraction must be in its lowest terms; $\frac{34}{60}$ alone does not score, and nor does the decimal `0.5\dot{6}`.

parts.problemMd:
The volume of liquid in a hemispherical bowl is given by the formula

`V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h^{2}\left(3R - h\right)`

where $R$ is the radius of the bowl and $h$ is the depth of liquid, that is, the height between the bottom of the bowl and the level of the liquid.

In a particular case, liquid is leaking through a small hole in the bottom of a bowl at a rate directly proportional to the depth of liquid.

When the bowl is full, the rate of volume loss is equal to $π$.

Show that the rate of change of the depth of the liquid is inversely proportional to `R\left(h - 2R\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
![Diagram of the hemispherical bowl, with the rim radius R shown by a horizontal arrow from the centre to the rim. A dashed ellipse partway down marks the liquid surface, and the depth of liquid h is shown by a vertical double-headed arrow from the bottom of the bowl up to that surface.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/differentiation/applications-of-differentiation/assets/008-diagram-of-the-hemispherical-bowl-with-the-rim-r.png)

"Directly proportional" becomes an equation once a constant is introduced. The liquid is leaking, so the volume is falling and the rate is negative

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = - k h$* for a positive constant *$k$

**[M1]**

That constant has to be found, we can use the information about when the bowl is full to find it

A hemispherical bowl is full when the liquid reaches the brim, so the depth is then the bowl's own radius, $h = R$. Losing volume at a rate of $π$ makes the rate $- π$

$- k R = - π   \Rightarrow   k = \frac{π}{R}$

**[M1]**

So the rate of volume loss is known in terms of the depth

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = - \frac{πh}{R}$

**[A1]**

Now the other rate. Expand the given formula so the power rule applies term by term, then differentiate with respect to the depth

`V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(3Rh^{2} - h^{3}\right) = \pi Rh^{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\pi h^{3}`

$\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = 2 π R h - π h^{2}$

**[M1]**

Factorise, since the target is a product

`\dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = \pi h\left(2R - h\right)`

**[A1]**

The chain rule links the two rates through the depth

`\dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} \times \dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; -\dfrac{\pi h}{R} = \pi h\left(2R - h\right) \times \dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}`

**[M1]**

Make the wanted rate the subject. The $π$ and the $h$ both cancel, which is what leaves the clean form

`\dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{-1}{R\left(2R - h\right)}`

Negating the bracket absorbs the minus sign and gives the form asked for

`\dfrac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{1}{R\left(h - 2R\right)}`

**Final answer:** **so the rate of change of depth is inversely proportional to **`R\left(h - 2R\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Translating the proportionality into an equation with a constant, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = - k h$, with the sign showing that volume is being lost.
> 
> **M1**: Using $h = R$ when the bowl is full, together with a rate of loss of $π$, to find your constant.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = - \frac{πh}{R}$.
> 
> **M1**: Expanding the given formula and differentiating with respect to $h$.
> 
> **A1**: $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} = 2 π R h - π h^{2}$, or the factorised $π h ( 2 R - h )$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} = \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}h} \times \frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching $\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = \frac{1}{R(h-2R)}$ and stating the conclusion that this is inversely proportional to $R ( h - 2 R )$. Because the result is given, any incorrect working loses this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Differentiate

(i) $5 x$,

(ii) $2 x^{3}$,

(iii) $x^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the power rule `\dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\left(ax^{n}\right) = anx^{n-1}` to each term

(i)

For the linear term, the gradient of $y = 5 x$ is simply its coefficient

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 5$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Multiply by the power $3$, then reduce the power by $1$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 6 x^{2}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The same rule applies to the fractional power $n = \frac{1}{2}$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct derivative of $5 x$, giving $5$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct derivative of $2 x^{3}$, giving $6 x^{2}$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct derivative of $x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, giving $\frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Accept any equivalent form, such as $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}$, and accept unsimplified answers.

may be written in the form

parts.solutionMd:

find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the function $y$ defined in part (a). Be sure to give your answer entirely in terms of $x$.

parts.problemMd:
Find the gradient at the point where $x = 8$ for the following functions

(i) $\text{f} ( x ) = 3 x^{2}$,

(ii) $\text{f} ( x ) = 4 x^{3} - 2 x$,

(iii) $\text{f} ( x ) = 3 x^{\frac{1}{3}}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate each function, then substitute $x = 8$ into the derivative

(i)

Differentiate $3 x^{2}$, then evaluate at $x = 8$

$\text{f} ' ( x ) = 6 x$

$\text{f} ' ( 8 ) = 6 ( 8 ) = 48$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Differentiate $4 x^{3} - 2 x$ term by term, then evaluate at $x = 8$

$\text{f} ' ( x ) = 12 x^{2} - 2$

$\text{f} ' ( 8 ) = 12 ( 8 )^{2} - 2 = 766$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Differentiate $3 x^{\frac{1}{3}}$ using the power rule, then evaluate at $x = 8$

`\text{f}'(x) = 3 \cdot \tfrac{1}{3}x^{-\frac{2}{3}} = x^{-\frac{2}{3}}`

`\text{f}'(8) = 8^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{\left(\sqrt[3]{8}\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{4}`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct gradient for (i), $\text{f} ' ( 8 ) = 48$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct gradient for (ii), $\text{f} ' ( 8 ) = 766$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct gradient for (iii), $\text{f} ' ( 8 ) = \frac{1}{4}$. Accept any exact equivalent, such as $8^{-\frac{2}{3}}$ or $0 . 25$.

By first defining an appropriate function $u$ and writing $y$ in the form $y = u^{n}$ where $n$ is a positive integer, use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ in terms of $x$.

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = x - 3$ back to give the answer in terms of $x$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4 ( x - 3 )^{3}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
(i) By solving the equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$, find the coordinates of any stationary points.

(ii) By considering the value of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ on either side of any stationary points, determine the nature of those stationary points.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Stationary points occur where the gradient is zero, so set $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$

$4 ( x - 3 )^{3} = 0  \Rightarrow  x = 3$

**[M1]**

Substitute $x = 3$ into $y = ( x - 3 )^{4}$ to find the $y$-coordinate

$( 3 ,  0 )$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Test the gradient just below the point, at $x = 2$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4 ( 2 - 3 )^{3} = - 4$

Test the gradient just above the point, at $x = 4$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4 ( 4 - 3 )^{3} = 4$

The gradient changes from negative to positive, so the curve turns upward

**Final answer:** $( 3 ,  0 )$** is a minimum point**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$ and solving to obtain $x = 3$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct stationary point $( 3 , 0 )$.
> 
> **B1**: Minimum correctly identified, justified by $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ changing from negative to positive across $x = 3$.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
Multiply both sides by $( x - 3 )$ to make $y$ the subject

parts.problemMd:
The curve with equation $y = a x^{2} + b x + c$ has a gradient of $- 7$ at the point $( - 1 , 13 )$, and a gradient of $- 3$ at the point $( 1 , 3 )$.

By considering $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ show that $2 a + b = - 3$ and $- 2 a + b = - 7$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the curve to obtain the gradient function

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 2 a x + b$

**[M1]**

At $( 1 , 3 )$ the gradient is $- 3$, so substitute $x = 1$

$2 a ( 1 ) + b = - 3$

$2 a + b = - 3$

At $( - 1 , 13 )$ the gradient is $- 7$, so substitute $x = - 1$

$2 a ( - 1 ) + b = - 7$

$- 2 a + b = - 7$

parts.problemMd: Hence find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
Add the two equations to eliminate $a$

$( 2 a + b ) + ( - 2 a + b ) = - 3 + ( - 7 )  \Rightarrow  2 b = - 10  \Rightarrow  b = - 5$

Substitute $b = - 5$ into $2 a + b = - 3$

$2 a - 5 = - 3  \Rightarrow  a = 1$

**Final answer:** $a = 1$** and **$b = - 5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both correct values, $a = 1$ and $b = - 5$.

parts.problemMd: Given that `y = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{x}\right)`, $x > 0$, find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$.

parts.problemMd: `y = \dfrac{1}{x^{5}}\left(x^{2} + \sqrt{x} - 1\right)`
parts.solutionMd:
Multiply out by dividing each term by $x^{5}$; first rewrite $\sqrt{x}$ as a power so every term is a power of $x$

`y = \dfrac{1}{x^{5}}\left(x^{2} + x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1\right)`

Divide each term in the bracket by $x^{5}$, subtracting the powers using $\frac{x^{a}}{x^{b}} = x^{a-b}$

$y = \frac{x^{2}}{x^{5}} + \frac{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{x^{5}} - \frac{1}{x^{5}} = x^{2-5} + x^{\frac{1}{2}-5} - x^{-5}$

Simplify each power

$y = x^{-3} + x^{-\frac{9}{2}} - x^{-5}$

**[M1]**

Differentiate each term, multiplying by the power and reducing it by $1$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 3 x^{-4} - \frac{9}{2} x^{-\frac{11}{2}} + 5 x^{-6}$

parts.problemMd:
For each of the following, use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ in terms of $x$:

`y = \left(\dfrac{1}{x} + 2x\right)^{4}`
parts.solutionMd:
Let the inner bracket be $u$, so $y$ becomes a power of $u$

$u = \frac{1}{x} + 2 x = x^{-1} + 2 x  \Rightarrow  y = u^{4}$

**[B1]**

Differentiate each part

$\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = - x^{-2} + 2$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = 4 u^{3}$

**[B1]**

Combine using the chain rule $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} \times \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}$

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4u^{3}\left(2 - x^{-2}\right)`

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = \frac{1}{x} + 2 x$ back

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + 2x\right)^{3}\left(2 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A suitable substitution, $u = \frac{1}{x} + 2 x$, giving $y = u^{4}$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct component derivatives, $\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = 2 - x^{-2}$ and $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = 4 u^{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, multiplying the two derivatives.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct derivative in terms of $x$. Accept unsimplified or equivalent forms.

parts.problemMd: `y = \dfrac{1}{\left(x^{3} - 1\right)^{2}}`

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 u^{-3} ( 3 x^{2} ) = - 6 x^{2} u^{-3}$

parts.problemMd: The function $\text{f}$ is defined by $\text{f} ( x ) = x^{3} - 4 x^{2} + 6 x - 9$. Show that there are no solutions to the equation $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$.

parts.problemMd:
A curve has the equation $y = \frac{3}{8} x^{\frac{4}{3}} - 12 x^{\frac{1}{3}}$.

Show that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = a  x^{-\frac{2}{3}} ( x + b )$, where $a$ and $b$ are rational numbers to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate each term, multiplying by the power and reducing it by $1$

Factor out the lower power $x^{-\frac{2}{3}}$ to reach the required form

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = x^{-\frac{2}{3}}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}x - 4\right) = \tfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{2}{3}}(x - 8)`

$a = \frac{1}{2} ,  b = - 8$

> **A1**: Correctly factored to $\frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{2}{3}} ( x - 8 )$, giving $a = \frac{1}{2}$ and $b = - 8$.

parts.problemMd: A curve has the equation $y = 4 x^{3} + b x^{2} + 3 x - 17$, where $b$ is a constant. Given that there is only one point on the curve where the gradient is zero, determine the possible values of $b$.

parts.problemMd: The curve with equation $y = a x^{2} + b x + c$ has a gradient of $8$ at the point $( - 2 , 0 )$, and a gradient of $- 10$ at the point $( 1 , - 3 )$. Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.

parts.problemMd: A curve has the equation $y = x \sqrt{x} + \frac{48}{\sqrt{x}}$, $x > 0$. Find the coordinates of the point on the curve where the gradient is $0$.

Expand the square using $( a - b )^{2} = a^{2} - 2 a b + b^{2}$

`y = \left(x^{-1}\right)^{2} - 2\left(x^{-1}\right)\left(x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right) + \left(x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right)^{2} = x^{-2} - 2x^{-\frac{5}{2}} + x^{-3}`

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 x^{-3} + 5 x^{-\frac{7}{2}} - 3 x^{-4}$

parts.problemMd:

$y = \frac{x(2x+1)(x-3)}{2x+1} = x ( x - 3 ) = x^{2} - 3 x$

Differentiate the simplified quadratic

**[A1]**

>

Rewrite $\frac{4}{\sqrt{x}}$ as a power, so the bracket is a sum of powers of $x$

`y = \left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 - 4x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2}`

Expand the square, squaring each term and adding twice each pairwise product

$y = x + 9 + 16 x^{-1} + 6 x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 8 - 24 x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Collect the constant terms $9 - 8 = 1$

parts.problemMd:
For each of the following, use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ in terms of $x$:

`y = \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + 3x^{2}\right)^{3}`
parts.solutionMd:
Let the inner bracket be $u$, so $y$ becomes a power of $u$

$u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + 3 x^{2} = x^{-\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x^{2}  \Rightarrow  y = u^{3}$

**[B1]**

Differentiate each part

$\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}} + 6 x$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = 3 u^{2}$

**[B1]**

Combine using the chain rule

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \left(6x - \tfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right)(3u^{2})`

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + 3 x^{2}$ back

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 3\left(6x - \dfrac{1}{2x\sqrt{x}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} + 3x^{2}\right)^{2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A suitable substitution, $u = x^{-\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x^{2}$, giving $y = u^{3}$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct component derivatives, $\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}} + 6 x$ and $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = 3 u^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, multiplying the two derivatives.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct derivative in terms of $x$. Accept unsimplified or equivalent forms.

parts.problemMd: $y = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}}}$
parts.solutionMd:
First rewrite the inner denominator as powers of $x$

$\sqrt{x} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Take the reciprocal (index $- 1$), then the outer square root (index $\frac{1}{2}$), multiplying the indices

`y = \sqrt{\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{-1}} = \left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}`

Let the inner bracket be $u$, so $y$ becomes a power of $u$

$u = x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}  \Rightarrow  y = u^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

**[B1]**

Differentiate each part

$\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}} - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = - \frac{1}{2} u^{-\frac{3}{2}}$

**[B1]**

Combine using the chain rule and simplify the constant

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{1}{2}} - \tfrac{1}{2}x^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right)\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}u^{-\frac{3}{2}}\right) = \tfrac{1}{4}\left(x^{-\frac{3}{2}} - x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)u^{-\frac{3}{2}}`

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ back

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \tfrac{1}{4}\left(x^{-\frac{3}{2}} - x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Rewriting $y$ as `\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}` with a suitable substitution.
> 
> **B1**: Correct component derivatives, $\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} = \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{1}{2}} - \frac{1}{2} x^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ and $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} = - \frac{1}{2} u^{-\frac{3}{2}}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, multiplying the two derivatives.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct derivative. Accept equivalent forms, including the simplified $\frac{1-x}{4x(x+1)} \sqrt{\frac{\sqrt{x}}{x+1}}$.

parts.problemMd: The function $\text{f}$ is defined by $\text{f} ( x ) = 2 x^{3} + p x^{2} + 3 x - 16$. Determine the range of values for $p$ for which the equation $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$ has at least one real solution.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate; $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$ is a quadratic in $x$

$\text{f} ' ( x ) = 6 x^{2} + 2 p x + 3$

**[M1]**

For this quadratic to have at least one real solution, its discriminant must be non-negative

$( 2 p )^{2} - 4 ( 6 ) ( 3 ) \geq 0$

**[M1]**

Simplify the inequality

$4 p^{2} - 72 \geq 0  \Rightarrow  p^{2} \geq 18$

**[A1]**

The critical values are $p = \pm \sqrt{18} = \pm 3 \sqrt{2}$, and $p^{2} \geq 18$ holds outside them

$p = \pm 3 \sqrt{2}$

**[M1]**

State the range of values

**Final answer:** $p \leq - 3 \sqrt{2}$** or **$p \geq 3 \sqrt{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct derivative, $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 6 x^{2} + 2 p x + 3$.
> 
> **M1**: Using the discriminant with $\geq 0$ for at least one real solution.
> 
> **A1**: Correct inequality, $4 p^{2} - 72 \geq 0$ (or $p^{2} \geq 18$).
> 
> **M1**: Solving the quadratic inequality, with critical values $p = \pm 3 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct range, $p \leq - 3 \sqrt{2}$ or $p \geq 3 \sqrt{2}$. Accept equivalent exact forms such as $\pm \sqrt{18}$.

parts.problemMd:
Given that `y = \left(\dfrac{1}{x} + x\right)^{4}`, $x \neq 0$

use the chain rule to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$
parts.solutionMd:
Let the inner bracket be $u$, so $y$ becomes a power of $u$

$u = \frac{1}{x} + x = x^{-1} + x  \Rightarrow  y = u^{4}$

**[B1]**

Differentiate each part and combine with the chain rule $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u} \times \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}$

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4u^{3}\left(1 - x^{-2}\right)`

**[M1]**

Substitute $u = \frac{1}{x} + x$ back

`\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 4\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + x\right)^{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A suitable substitution, $u = \frac{1}{x} + x$, giving $y = u^{4}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the chain rule, $4 u^{3} \times ( 1 - x^{-2} )$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct derivative, `4\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + x\right)^{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right)`.

parts.problemMd: Find the coordinates of any stationary points and determine their nature.
parts.solutionMd:
Stationary points occur where $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$; set each factor to zero in turn

`4\left(\dfrac{1 + x^{2}}{x}\right)^{3}\left(\dfrac{x^{2} - 1}{x^{2}}\right) = 0`

$1 + x^{2} = 0$ has no real solution, so solve $x^{2} - 1 = 0$

$x^{2} - 1 = 0  \Rightarrow  x = \pm 1$

**[M1]**

Find each $y$-coordinate

$x = 1 :  y = ( 1 + 1 )^{4} = 16$

$x = - 1 :  y = ( - 1 - 1 )^{4} = 16$

**Final answer:** $( 1 ,  16 )$** and **$( - 1 ,  16 )$

**[A1]**

There is an asymptote at $x = 0$ ($x \neq 0$), so test the gradient sign either side of each stationary point

| $x$ | $- 2$ | $- \frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

**[M1]**

Both show the gradient changing from negative to positive

**Final answer:** $( 1 , 16 )$** and **$( - 1 , 16 )$** are both minimum points**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 0$ and solving to obtain $x = \pm 1$ (rejecting $1 + x^{2} = 0$).
> 
> **A1**: Both correct stationary points, $( 1 , 16 )$ and $( - 1 , 16 )$.
> 
> **M1**: Testing the sign of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ either side of each stationary point.
> 
> **A1**: Both correctly identified as minimum points.

parts.solutionMd:

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd: The function $\text{f}$ is defined by $\text{f} ( x ) = x^{n} - x$, $n \in ℕ$, $n \geq 2$. Determine the relationship between the value of $n$ and the number of real solutions to the equation $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate and set $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$

$\text{f} ' ( x ) = n x^{n-1} - 1 = 0  \Rightarrow  x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}$

**[M1 A1]**

Taking the $( n - 1 )$th root gives the general solution

`x = \left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-1}}`

Work through the first few values of $n$, solving $x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}$ each time; an even power gives two roots (from $\pm$), an odd power gives one

| $n$ | $x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}$ | Solve for $x$ | Real roots |
|---|---|---|---|
| $2$ | $x^{1} = \frac{1}{2}$ | $x = \frac{1}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $3$ | $x^{2} = \frac{1}{3}$ | $x = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $2$ |
| $4$ | $x^{3} = \frac{1}{4}$ | `x = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]{4}}` | $1$ |
| $5$ | $x^{4} = \frac{1}{5}$ | `x = \pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt[4]{5}}` | $2$ |

**[M1]**

The count follows the parity of $n - 1$: when $n$ is even $n - 1$ is odd (one root), and when $n$ is odd $n - 1$ is even (two roots)

**Final answer:** $n$** even: one real solution; **$n$** odd: two real solutions**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiating and setting $\text{f} ' ( x ) = 0$ (power decreased by 1).
> 
> **A1**: Correct rearrangement, $x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving $x^{n-1} = \frac{1}{n}$ for several values of $n$ (or reasoning from the parity of $n - 1$) to find the number of real roots in each case.
> 
> **A1**: Correct relationship — one real solution when $n$ is even, two real solutions when $n$ is odd.

parts.problemMd: A curve is described by the equation $\frac{\sqrt{y}}{-1+\sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{x}$, $x > 1$. Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Make $y$ the subject: rearrange for $\sqrt{y}$, then square both sides

$\sqrt{y} = \frac{-1+\sqrt{x}}{x}  \Rightarrow  y = \frac{(-1+\sqrt{x})^{2}}{x^{2}}$

Expand the numerator, writing $\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}$

$y = \frac{1-2\sqrt{x}+x}{x^{2}} = \frac{1-2x^{\frac{1}{2}}+x}{x^{2}}$

Divide each term by $x^{2}$, subtracting the powers

$y = \frac{1}{x^{2}} - \frac{2x^{\frac{1}{2}}}{x^{2}} + \frac{x}{x^{2}} = x^{-2} - 2 x^{-\frac{3}{2}} + x^{-1}$

**[M1 A1]**

Differentiate each term, multiplying by the power and reducing it by $1$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = - 2 x^{-3} + 3 x^{-\frac{5}{2}} - x^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Making $y$ the subject and expanding to a sum of powers of $x$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct form, $y = x^{-2} - 2 x^{-\frac{3}{2}} + x^{-1}$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct derivative, $- 2 x^{-3} + 3 x^{-\frac{5}{2}} - x^{-2}$. Accept unsimplified equivalents.

parts.problemMd: The curve with equation $y = a x^{2} + b x + c$ passes through the point $( - 1 , 4 )$. At the point $( 2 , 7 )$ the gradient of the curve is $7$. Find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
parts.solutionMd:
The point $( - 1 , 4 )$ lies on the curve, so substitute it in

$4 = a ( - 1 )^{2} + b ( - 1 ) + c  \Rightarrow  a - b + c = 4$* (1)*

The point $( 2 , 7 )$ also lies on the curve

$7 = a ( 2 )^{2} + b ( 2 ) + c  \Rightarrow  4 a + 2 b + c = 7$* (2)*

**[M1 A1]**

Differentiate; the gradient at $( 2 , 7 )$ is $7$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} = 2 a x + b  \Rightarrow  4 a + b = 7$* (3)*

**[M1]**

Subtract $( 1 ) - ( 2 )$ to eliminate $c$, giving $a + b = 1$, then combine with $( 3 )$

$a + b = 1$* and *$4 a + b = 7$

$a = 2 ,  b = - 1$

**[A1]**

Substitute $a = 2$ and $b = - 1$ into $( 1 )$ to find $c$

$2 - ( - 1 ) + c = 4$

$a = 2 ,  b = - 1 ,  c = 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting both points into $y = a x^{2} + b x + c$ to form two equations.
> 
> **A1**: Both correct equations, $a - b + c = 4$ and $4 a + 2 b + c = 7$.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiating to $2 a x + b$ and using the gradient condition to form $4 a + b = 7$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct values $a = 2$ and $b = - 1$ from solving simultaneously.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value, $c = 1$.

parts.problemMd:
The area bounded by the curve with equation $y = 9 - x^{2}$, the $x$-axis and the vertical lines with equations $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ is to be found.

Write down an integral that would find this area.
parts.solutionMd:
The area between a curve and the $x$-axis is found by integrating the equation of the curve, and the two vertical lines give the limits

`\int_{1}^{2} \left(9 - x^{2}\right) \,\text{d}x`

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct integrand $9 - x^{2}$, written with $\text{d} x$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct limits, with $1$ at the bottom of the integral sign and $2$ at the top.
> 
> You do not need to evaluate the integral to earn these marks.

parts.problemMd: Evaluate your integral from part (a) and hence find the area described above.
parts.solutionMd:
To evaluate the integral, integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`\int_{1}^{2} \left(9 - x^{2}\right) \,\text{d}x = \left[\,9x - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\,\right]_{1}^{2}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \left(9(2) - \dfrac{(2)^{3}}{3}\right) - \left(9(1) - \dfrac{(1)^{3}}{3}\right)`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket, writing both as thirds so they can be subtracted

`= \left(18 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(9 - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{46}{3} - \dfrac{26}{3}`

**Final answer:** $\frac{20}{3}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct integration of both terms to give $9 x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $2$ and $1$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit.
> 
> **A1**: Correct area $\frac{20}{3}$ square units. Answers which round to $6 . 67$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y = 7 x - x^{2} - 6$.

![Graph of the parabola y = 7x − x² − 6, opening downwards and crossing the x-axis at (1, 0) and (6, 0), with the region between these points and above the x-axis shaded and labelled R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/002-graph-of-the-parabola-y-7x-x-6-opening-downwards.png)

Find the shaded area, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest terms.
parts.solutionMd:
The shaded region lies above the $x$-axis between the two points where the curve crosses it, and the diagram gives these as $x = 1$ and $x = 6$, so they are the limits

`\text{Area} = \int_{1}^{6} \left(7x - x^{2} - 6\right) \,\text{d}x`

Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`= \left[\,\dfrac{7x^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3} - 6x\,\right]_{1}^{6}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \left(\dfrac{7(6)^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{(6)^{3}}{3} - 6(6)\right) - \left(\dfrac{7(1)^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{(1)^{3}}{3} - 6(1)\right)`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket, taking care with the signs when subtracting the negative lower value

`= \left(126 - 72 - 36\right) - \left(\dfrac{7}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3} - 6\right) = 18 - \left(-\dfrac{17}{6}\right)`

**Final answer:** $\frac{125}{6}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct integration of all three terms to give $\frac{7x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 6 x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $6$ and $1$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit. The limits are labelled on the diagram, so you are not required to solve $7 x - x^{2} - 6 = 0$ to find them.
> 
> **A1**: Correct area $\frac{125}{6}$ square units. The question asks for a fraction in its simplest terms, so a decimal answer is not accepted here.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the graph of $y = x^{2} - 8 x + 12$.

![Graph of the parabola y = x² − 8x + 12, opening upwards and crossing the x-axis at (2, 0) and (6, 0), with the region between these points and below the x-axis shaded and labelled R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/005-graph-of-the-parabola-y-x-8x-12-opening-upwards-.png)

parts.solutionMd:
The diagram gives the points where the curve crosses the $x$-axis as $x = 2$ and $x = 6$, so these are the limits

Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`\int_{2}^{6} \left(x^{2} - 8x + 12\right) \,\text{d}x = \left[\,\dfrac{x^{3}}{3} - 4x^{2} + 12x\,\right]_{2}^{6}`

**[M1 A1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

Work out each bracket

The region lies below the $x$-axis, which is why the integral has come out negative, so take the modulus to make the area positive

**Final answer:** $\frac{32}{3}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

Your final answer must be positive, so you also earn this mark if you work out $- \frac{32}{3}$ from the integral and then change it to $+ \frac{32}{3}$. If you leave your answer as $- \frac{32}{3}$ you do not earn this mark. The question asks for a fraction in its simplest form, so a decimal answer is not accepted here.

parts.problemMd: Simplify `x - \left(x^{2} - 8x + 18\right)`.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the bracket, remembering that the minus sign in front of it changes the sign of every term inside

`x - \left(x^{2} - 8x + 18\right) = x - x^{2} + 8x - 18`

Collect the two terms in $x$

$9 x - x^{2} - 18$

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $y = x^{2} - 8 x + 18$ and $y = x$.

![Graph showing the upward-opening parabola y = x² − 8x + 18 and the straight line y = x, which intersect at (3, 3) and (6, 6), with the region between the line and the curve shaded and labelled R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/003-graph-showing-the-upward-opening-parabola-y-x-8x.png)

Find the shaded area marked $R$, giving your answer as a fraction in its simplest terms.
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram gives the two points where the line meets the curve as $( 3 , 3 )$ and $( 6 , 6 )$, so the limits are $x = 3$ and $x = 6$

Between these limits the line lies above the curve, so the area is found by integrating (line $-$ curve), which is exactly the expression simplified in part (a)

`\text{Area} = \int_{3}^{6} \left(9x - x^{2} - 18\right) \,\text{d}x`

Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`= \left[\,\dfrac{9x^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3} - 18x\,\right]_{3}^{6}`

**[M1 A1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \left(\dfrac{9(6)^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{(6)^{3}}{3} - 18(6)\right) - \left(\dfrac{9(3)^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{(3)^{3}}{3} - 18(3)\right)`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket, taking care with the signs when subtracting the negative lower value

`= \left(162 - 72 - 108\right) - \left(\dfrac{81}{2} - 9 - 54\right) = -18 - \left(-\dfrac{45}{2}\right)`

**Final answer:** $\frac{9}{2}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: A clear attempt to integrate, with the index of at least one term increased by $1$.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct integrated expression $\frac{9x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3} - 18 x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $6$ and $3$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit.
> 
> **A1**: Correct area $\frac{9}{2}$ square units. Your integrand must be (line $-$ curve). Integrating (curve $-$ line) gives $- \frac{9}{2}$, which does not earn this mark, since an area must be positive. The question asks for a fraction in its simplest terms, so a decimal answer is not accepted here.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the region $R$, bounded by the straight lines with equations $y = 2 x + 1$, $x = 2$, $x = 4$ and the $x$-axis.

![Graph of the straight line y = 2x + 1, with the region R shaded between the line, the x-axis, and the vertical lines x = 2 and x = 4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/001-graph-of-the-straight-line-y-2x-1-with-the-regio.png)

(i) For $y = 2 x + 1$, show that $y^{2} = 4 x^{2} + 4 x + 1$.

(ii) Find the volume of the solid formed when the region $R$ is rotated 360° around the $x$-axis.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Square both sides and expand the bracket

`y^{2} = \left(2x + 1\right)^{2} = 4x^{2} + 2x + 2x + 1`

Collect the two terms in $x$ to reach the required result

**Final answer:** $y^{2} = 4 x^{2} + 4 x + 1$** as required**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The volume formed by rotating a region through 360° about the $x$-axis is found using

`V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} y^{2} \,\text{d}x`

The region is bounded by $x = 2$ and $x = 4$, so these are the limits, and part (i) has already given $y^{2}$

`V = \pi \int_{2}^{4} \left(4x^{2} + 4x + 1\right) \,\text{d}x`

**[M1]**

Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`= \pi \left[\,\dfrac{4x^{3}}{3} + 2x^{2} + x\,\right]_{2}^{4}`

**[A1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \pi \left[\left(\dfrac{4(4)^{3}}{3} + 2(4)^{2} + 4\right) - \left(\dfrac{4(2)^{3}}{3} + 2(2)^{2} + 2\right)\right]`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket, writing both as thirds so they can be subtracted

`= \pi \left[\left(\dfrac{256}{3} + 36\right) - \left(\dfrac{32}{3} + 10\right)\right] = \pi \left(\dfrac{364}{3} - \dfrac{62}{3}\right)`

**Final answer:** $\frac{302π}{3}$** cubic units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct expansion of `\left(2x + 1\right)^{2}` leading to the given result $4 x^{2} + 4 x + 1$. The result is given to you, so your working must show the expansion, for example the middle step $4 x^{2} + 2 x + 2 x + 1$. Simply writing the answer down does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of `V = \pi \int y^{2} \,\text{d}x` with the limits $2$ and $4$, integrating $y^{2}$ rather than $y$. A missing $π$ at this stage is condoned.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct integrated expression $\frac{4x^{3}}{3} + 2 x^{2} + x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $4$ and $2$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit.
> 
> **A1**: Correct volume $\frac{302π}{3}$ cubic units. Your final answer must include $π$. Answers which round to $316$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the curve with equation $y = x^{2} + 2$. The shaded region $R$ is bounded by the curve, the $y$-axis and the lines $y = 6$ and $y = 11$.

![Graph of the upward-opening parabola y = x² + 2 with the horizontal lines y = 6 and y = 11 drawn across it, and the region R shaded between the y-axis, the right-hand branch of the curve, and the two horizontal lines](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/004-graph-of-the-upward-opening-parabola-y-x-2-with-.png)

Find the volume of the solid formed when the shaded region $R$ is rotated through 360° about the $y$-axis.
parts.solutionMd:
The rotation is about the $y$-axis, so the volume formula integrates $x^{2}$ with respect to $y$

`V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} x^{2} \,\text{d}y`

This means the equation of the curve has to be rearranged to give $x^{2}$ in terms of $y$

$y = x^{2} + 2 \Rightarrow x^{2} = y - 2$

**[M1]**

The region is bounded by the lines $y = 6$ and $y = 11$, so these are the limits

`V = \pi \int_{6}^{11} \left(y - 2\right) \,\text{d}y`

**[M1]**

Integrate with respect to $y$, increasing the index of each term by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`= \pi \left[\,\dfrac{y^{2}}{2} - 2y\,\right]_{6}^{11}`

**[A1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \pi \left[\left(\dfrac{(11)^{2}}{2} - 2(11)\right) - \left(\dfrac{(6)^{2}}{2} - 2(6)\right)\right]`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket

`= \pi \left[\left(\dfrac{121}{2} - 22\right) - \left(18 - 12\right)\right] = \pi \left(\dfrac{77}{2} - 6\right)`

**Final answer:** $\frac{65π}{2}$** cubic units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement of the equation of the curve to give $x^{2} = y - 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of `V = \pi \int x^{2} \,\text{d}y` with the limits $6$ and $11$. A missing $π$ at this stage is condoned. Because the rotation is about the $y$-axis you must integrate $x^{2}$ with respect to $y$. Integrating $y^{2}$ with respect to $x$, or integrating before rearranging, earns no further marks.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct integrated expression $\frac{y^{2}}{2} - 2 y$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $11$ and $6$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit.
> 
> **A1**: Correct volume $\frac{65π}{2}$ cubic units. Your final answer must include $π$. Answers which round to $102$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows part of the graph of $y = x^{2} - 4 x + 3$.

Find the area of the shaded region labelled $R$.

![Graph of the upward-opening parabola y = x² − 4x + 3, crossing the x-axis at x = 1 and x = 3, with the region between these points and below the x-axis shaded and labelled R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/031-graph-of-the-upward-opening-parabola-y-x-4x-3-cr.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram gives the points where the curve crosses the $x$-axis as $x = 1$ and $x = 3$, so these are the limits

Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`\int_{1}^{3} \left(x^{2} - 4x + 3\right) \,\text{d}x = \left[\,\dfrac{x^{3}}{3} - 2x^{2} + 3x\,\right]_{1}^{3}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \left(\dfrac{(3)^{3}}{3} - 2(3)^{2} + 3(3)\right) - \left(\dfrac{(1)^{3}}{3} - 2(1)^{2} + 3(1)\right)`

**[M1]**

Work out each bracket

`= \left(9 - 18 + 9\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 2 + 3\right) = 0 - \dfrac{4}{3} = -\dfrac{4}{3}`

The region lies below the $x$-axis, which is why the integral has come out negative, so take the modulus to make the area positive

`\text{Area of } R = \left|-\dfrac{4}{3}\right|`

**Final answer:** $\frac{4}{3}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct integration of all three terms to give $\frac{x^{3}}{3} - 2 x^{2} + 3 x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the limits $3$ and $1$ into your integrated expression, with the value at the lower limit subtracted from the value at the upper limit. The limits are labelled on the diagram, so you are not required to solve $x^{2} - 4 x + 3 = 0$ to find them.
> 
> **A1**: Correct area $\frac{4}{3}$ square units. Because the region is below the $x$-axis the integral gives $- \frac{4}{3}$; you still earn this mark if you then change it to $+ \frac{4}{3}$, but not if you leave your final answer negative. Answers which round to $1 . 33$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:

Write down the values of $x$ where $y = 0$.
parts.solutionMd:

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd:
Show that

`4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2} = 4x - x^{2}`
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the squared bracket

`4 - \left(x - 2\right)^{2} = 4 - \left(x^{2} - 4x + 4\right)`

Remove the bracket, remembering that the minus sign in front of it changes the sign of every term inside

$= 4 - x^{2} + 4 x - 4$

The two $4$s cancel, leaving the required result

**Final answer:** $= 4 x - x^{2}$** as required**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct expansion of `\left(x - 2\right)^{2}` and simplification leading to the given result $4 x - x^{2}$. The result is given to you, so your working must show the expansion. Writing the answer down on its own does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

`\int_{0}^{4} \left(4x - x^{2}\right) \,\text{d}x`
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`\int_{0}^{4} \left(4x - x^{2}\right) \,\text{d}x = \left[\,2x^{2} - \dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\,\right]_{0}^{4}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits, remembering that every term at the lower limit is $0$, so only the upper limit contributes

`= \left(2(4)^{2} - \dfrac{(4)^{3}}{3}\right) - 0 = 32 - \dfrac{64}{3}`

$\frac{32}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct integration of both terms to give $2 x^{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $\frac{32}{3}$. Answers which round to $10 . 7$ are also accepted.

parts.problemMd: Write down the area of the region labelled $R$.
parts.solutionMd:
The region $R$ lies between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$, the values found in part (a), so its area is the integral of the curve between those limits. Part (b) rewrote the curve as $4 x - x^{2}$, and part (c) has already evaluated exactly that integral

parts.problemMd: Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the line with equation $y = 2$ and the curve with equation $y = x^{2} - 4 x + 5$.
parts.solutionMd:
The line and the curve meet where their $y$-values are equal, so set the two equations equal to each other

$x^{2} - 4 x + 5 = 2$

Rearrange so that the quadratic equals zero, then factorise

$x^{2} - 4 x + 3 = 0$

`\left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 3\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Each bracket gives a solution

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd:
Evaluate

`\int_{1}^{3} \left(x^{2} - 4x + 5\right) \,\text{d}x`
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate each term by increasing its index by $1$ and dividing by the new index

`\int_{1}^{3} \left(x^{2} - 4x + 5\right) \,\text{d}x = \left[\,\dfrac{x^{3}}{3} - 2x^{2} + 5x\,\right]_{1}^{3}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the upper limit and then the lower limit into the integrated expression, and subtract

`= \left(\dfrac{(3)^{3}}{3} - 2(3)^{2} + 5(3)\right) - \left(\dfrac{(1)^{3}}{3} - 2(1)^{2} + 5(1)\right)`

Work out each bracket

`= \left(9 - 18 + 15\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{3} - 2 + 5\right) = 6 - \dfrac{10}{3}`

$\frac{8}{3}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct integration of all three terms to give $\frac{x^{3}}{3} - 2 x^{2} + 5 x$, with the limits $3$ and $1$ substituted and subtracted.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $\frac{8}{3}$. Answers which round to $2 . 67$ are also accepted.

The region between the line and the curve is shaded and labelled R](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/025-graph-of-the-upward-opening-parabola-y-x-4x-5-an.png)

Find the exact area of the shaded region $R$.
parts.solutionMd:
Between the intersections found in part (a) the line $y = 2$ lies above the curve, so the shaded region is what is left when the area under the curve is removed from the area under the line

The area under the line $y = 2$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$ is just a rectangle, of height $2$ and width $3 - 1 = 2$

$\text{Area under the line} = 2 \times 2 = 4$

**[M1]**

The area under the curve between those same limits is exactly the integral already evaluated in part (b)

$\text{Area of} R = 4 - \frac{8}{3}$

**[M1]**

Write both as thirds and subtract

$= \frac{12}{3} - \frac{8}{3}$

> **M1**: Correct method for the shaded region: your area under the line minus your answer to part (b).

> **A1**: Correct exact area $\frac{4}{3}$ square units. The question asks for the exact area, so a decimal answer is not accepted here.

> Alternative method: you can instead integrate (line $-$ curve) directly, `\int_{1}^{3} \left(2 - \left(x^{2} - 4x + 5\right)\right) \,\text{d}x = \int_{1}^{3} \left(-x^{2} + 4x - 3\right) \,\text{d}x`. parts.problemMd:
The diagram below shows the graphs of the line $y = 6 - x$ and the curve $y = x^{2}$.

![Graph of the curve y = x² and the line y = 6 − x. The curve passes through the origin, labelled P; the line and curve meet at a point labelled Q; the line crosses the x-axis at a point labelled R. The region bounded by the curve from P to Q, the line from Q to R, and the x-axis from P to R is shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/029-graph-of-the-curve-y-x-and-the-line-y-6-x-the-cu.png)

Find the $x$-coordinates of the points labelled $P$, $Q$ and $R$.
parts.solutionMd:
$P$ is where the curve $y = x^{2}$ meets the $x$-axis, which is the origin

$Q$ is where the line meets the curve, so set the two equations equal to each other

$x^{2} = 6 - x$

Rearrange so that the quadratic equals zero, then factorise

`x^{2} + x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow \left(x + 3\right)\left(x - 2\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

This gives $x = - 3$ and $x = 2$, and the diagram shows $Q$ to the right of the $y$-axis, so $Q$ is the positive root

$R$ is where the line meets the $x$-axis, so set $y = 0$

$6 - x = 0 \Rightarrow x = 6$

$P : x = 0$

$Q : x = 2$

$R : x = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting the line equal to the curve and rearranging to $x^{2} + x - 6 = 0$, then attempting to solve. Factorising, completing the square or the quadratic formula are all accepted.
> 
> **A1**: All three correct values $x = 0$, $x = 2$ and $x = 6$. The negative root $x = - 3$ is not one of the labelled points, because the diagram places $Q$ to the right of the $y$-axis, so it should be rejected.

parts.problemMd: Find the area of the shaded region.
parts.solutionMd:
The curve forms the top of the shaded region from $P$ to $Q$, and the line forms it from $Q$ to $R$, so split the region at $x = 2$ and find the two pieces separately

![Sketch of the shaded region with a dashed vertical line drawn at x = 2, running from the x-axis up to Q, showing where the region is split. The piece to the left of the dashed line, lying under the curve between P and Q, is shaded darker. The triangular piece to the right, lying under the line between Q and R, is shaded lighter. P, Q and R are labelled with their coordinates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/integration/further-integration/assets/030-sketch-of-the-shaded-region-with-a-dashed-vertic.png)

For the first piece, integrate the curve between $x = 0$ and $x = 2$

`\int_{0}^{2} x^{2} \,\text{d}x = \left[\,\dfrac{x^{3}}{3}\,\right]_{0}^{2} = \dfrac{(2)^{3}}{3} - \dfrac{(0)^{3}}{3}`

**[M1]**

$= \frac{8}{3}$

**[A1]**

The second piece is a right-angled triangle, so it needs no integration: its base runs from $x = 2$ to $x = 6$, and its height is the $y$-coordinate of $Q$

$\text{Area of triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 4 = 8$

**[M1]**

Add the two pieces, writing both as thirds

$\text{Area} = \frac{8}{3} + 8 = \frac{8}{3} + \frac{24}{3}$

**Final answer:** $\frac{32}{3}$** square units**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **A1**: Correct area under the curve, $\frac{8}{3}$.

> 
> **A1**: Correct total area $\frac{32}{3}$ square units. Answers which round to $10 . 7$ are also accepted. The two pieces must be added, because the region is a single area made of two parts, not a difference between two boundaries.

Find the $x$-coordinates of the points of intersection of the two graphs.
parts.solutionMd:
The curves meet where their $y$-values are equal, so set the two equations equal to each other

$x^{2} - 3 x + 4 = 4 - x^{2} + 2 x$

Collect every term on one side, noting that the $4$s cancel

$2 x^{2} - 5 x = 0$

Factorise, taking out the common factor of $x$

`x\left(2x - 5\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Each factor gives a solution

**Final answer:** $x = 0$** and **$x = \frac{5}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting the two equations equal to each other and rearranging to $2 x^{2} - 5 x = 0$, then attempting to solve. Factorising or the quadratic formula are both accepted.
