(i) Show that the angle between the sides of length $4$ cm and $5$ cm has $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{8}$.

(ii) Find the value of $\text{cos}  θ$ for each of the other two angles.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle with sides of length 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/042-triangle-with-sides-of-length-4-cm-5-cm-and-6-cm.png)

(i)

The angle between the sides of length $4$ and $5$ is opposite the side of length $6$, so rearrange the cosine rule for that angle

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{4^{2}+5^{2}-6^{2}}{2(4)(5)} = \frac{5}{40}$

**[M1]**

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{8}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

For the angle opposite the side of length $4$ (between the sides $5$ and $6$)

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{5^{2}+6^{2}-4^{2}}{2(5)(6)} = \frac{45}{60} = \frac{3}{4}$

For the angle opposite the side of length $5$ (between the sides $4$ and $6$)

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{4^{2}+6^{2}-5^{2}}{2(4)(6)} = \frac{27}{48} = \frac{9}{16}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement of the cosine rule for the angle opposite the side of length $6$, $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{4^{2}+5^{2}-6^{2}}{2(4)(5)}$.
> 
> **A1**: $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{1}{8}$, as required (accept $\frac{5}{40}$ simplified).
> 
> **B1**: Both other values correct, $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{9}{16}$.

parts.problemMd:
Two different triangles each have $A B = 5 . 3$ cm, $B C = 6 . 4$ cm and angle $A C B = 38 ^{\circ}$.

(i) Show that angle $B A C = 132 ^{\circ}$, correct to 3 significant figures, for one of the triangles.

(ii) Find angle $A B C$ for the other triangle.
parts.solutionMd:
The information (two sides and a non-included angle) gives two possible triangles — the acute case and the obtuse case

![The ambiguous case shown as one figure: apex B with BA = 5.3 cm; the side BC = 6.4 cm reaches a base line through A at two positions of C, each with a 38° angle at C — giving the acute triangle (angle BAC = 48°) and the obtuse triangle (angle BAC = 132°).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/047-the-ambiguous-case-shown-as-one-figure-apex-b-wi.png)

(i)

$B A C$ is opposite $B C = 6 . 4$ and the $38 ^{\circ}$ angle is opposite $A B = 5 . 3$. Arrange the sine rule with the sines on top

$\frac{\text{sin}BAC}{6.4} = \frac{\text{sin}38^{\circ}}{5.3}$

$\text{sin}  B A C = \frac{6.4\text{sin}38^{\circ}}{5.3} = 0 . 7434 \dots$

**[M1]**

The acute solution is

$\text{sin}^{-1}(0.7434\dots)=48.0^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

By the symmetry of the sine graph, $\text{sin}  B A C = \text{sin}  ( 180 ^{\circ} - B A C )$, so the obtuse angle is also possible

$B A C = 180 ^{\circ} - 48 . 0 ^{\circ} = 131 . 98 \dots ^{\circ}$

$B A C = 132 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

The other triangle uses the acute value $B A C = 48 . 0 ^{\circ}$. The angles sum to $180 ^{\circ}$

$A B C = 180 ^{\circ} - 38 ^{\circ} - 48 . 0 ^{\circ}$

$A B C = 94 . 0 ^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the sine rule to find $\text{sin}  B A C$, for example $\frac{\text{sin}BAC}{6.4} = \frac{\text{sin}38^{\circ}}{5.3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acute angle, answers which round to $48 . 0 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Obtaining $B A C = 132 ^{\circ}$ from $180 ^{\circ} - 48 . 0 ^{\circ}$ (using $\text{sin}  B A C = \text{sin}  ( 180 ^{\circ} - B A C )$).
> 
> **B1**: $A B C = 94 . 0 ^{\circ}$ for the other triangle (answers which round to $94 . 0 ^{\circ}$).

parts.problemMd:
A triangular field has an area of $10$ m². Two of its sides have lengths $3 . 2$ m and $8 . 4$ m, and the angle between them is $θ$.

Show that one possible value of $θ$ is $48 . 1 ^{\circ}$, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle with two sides 3.2 m and 8.4 m enclosing the angle θ, with the area labelled 10 m².](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/044-triangle-with-two-sides-3-2-m-and-8-4-m-enclosin.png)

The angle $θ$ is between the two known sides, so substitute into the area formula and equate to $10$

$\frac{1}{2} ( 3 . 2 ) ( 8 . 4 )  \text{sin}  θ = 10$

**[M1]**

$\text{sin}  θ = \frac{10}{13.44} = 0 . 7440 \dots$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse sine

$θ = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 7440 \dots ) = 48 . 070 \dots ^{\circ}$

$θ = 48 . 1 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula equated to $10$, $\frac{1}{2} ( 3 . 2 ) ( 8 . 4 )  \text{sin}  θ = 10$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $\text{sin}  θ = 0 . 744$ (answers which round to $0 . 744$).
> 
> **A1**: $θ = 48 . 1 ^{\circ}$ reached from an unrounded value (for example $48 . 07 ^{\circ}$), as required.

parts.problemMd: Show that there is another possible value of $θ$. You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
The area only fixes $\text{sin}  θ$, and by the symmetry of the sine graph $\text{sin}  θ = \text{sin}  ( 180 ^{\circ} - θ )$, so an obtuse angle gives the same area

$θ = 180 ^{\circ} - 48 . 07 \dots ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$θ = 131 . 9 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising a second solution from the symmetry of the sine graph, $\text{sin}  θ = \text{sin}  ( 180 ^{\circ} - θ )$, so $θ = 180 ^{\circ} - 48 . 07 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: $θ = 131 . 9 ^{\circ}$ (answers which round to $131 . 9 ^{\circ}$).

parts.problemMd: Using $θ = 48 . 1 ^{\circ}$, calculate the perimeter of the field, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the third side, which is opposite $θ$, using the cosine rule

$c^{2} = 3 . 2^{2} + 8 . 4^{2} - 2 ( 3 . 2 ) ( 8 . 4 )  \text{cos}  48 . 1 ^{\circ}$

$c^{2} = 44 . 90 \dots \Rightarrow c = 6 . 701 \dots$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the three sides for the perimeter

$P = 3 . 2 + 8 . 4 + 6 . 701 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 18 . 3$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the cosine rule for the third side, $c^{2} = 3 . 2^{2} + 8 . 4^{2} - 2 ( 3 . 2 ) ( 8 . 4 )  \text{cos}  48 . 1 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct third side (answers which round to $6 . 70$ m).
> 
> **A1**: Perimeter $= 18 . 3$ m, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $A B C$ has $A B = x$ cm, $A C = ( x + 8 )$ cm and angle $B A C = 150 ^{\circ}$. The area of the triangle is $2 \frac{1}{4}$ cm².

Show that $x$ satisfies the equation $x^{2} + 8 x = 9$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = x cm and AC = (x + 8) cm enclosing angle BAC = 150°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/045-triangle-abc-with-ab-x-cm-and-ac-x-8-cm-enclosin.png)

The angle $150 ^{\circ}$ is enclosed by the sides $A B$ and $A C$, so use the area formula with $\text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$

$\frac{1}{2}  x ( x + 8 )  \text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = 2 \frac{1}{4}$

**[M1]**

$\frac{1}{4}  x ( x + 8 ) = \frac{9}{4}$

**[A1]**

Multiply both sides by $4$ and expand

$x^{2} + 8 x = 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula with $\text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$, equated to $2 \frac{1}{4}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified equation, for example $\frac{1}{4} x ( x + 8 ) = \frac{9}{4}$.
> 
> **A1**: Reaching the printed result $x^{2} + 8 x = 9$ with correct working.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
Rearrange and factorise

$x^{2} + 8 x - 9 = 0 \Rightarrow ( x + 9 ) ( x - 1 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

A length must be positive, so reject $x = - 9$

$x = 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method to solve the quadratic, for example factorising to $( x + 9 ) ( x - 1 ) = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 1$, with $x = - 9$ rejected because a length must be positive.

parts.problemMd: Find the perimeter of the triangle, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = x cm and AC = (x + 8) cm enclosing angle BAC = 150°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/045-triangle-abc-with-ab-x-cm-and-ac-x-8-cm-enclosin.png)

$B C = 9 . 879 \dots$

**[A1]**

Add the three sides

**Final answer:** $\text{Perimeter} = 1 + 9 + 9 . 879 \dots = 19 . 9$** cm**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd: Write the ratio of the angles of the triangle, to the nearest degree, in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = 1 cm and AC = 9 cm enclosing the angle 150°, and the third side BC = 9.88 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/046-triangle-abc-with-ab-1-cm-and-ac-9-cm-enclosing-.png)

One angle is $150 ^{\circ}$. Find a second angle with the sine rule — angle $C$ is opposite $A B = 1$

parts.problemMd:
The Save My Exams logo is a blue circle with a black lightning bolt through the centre. The lightning bolt is modelled as two congruent triangles $A B C$ and $D E F$ with $A B = D E = 12$ cm, $B C = E F = 15$ cm and $A C = D F = 7$ cm.

![The Save My Exams circular logo with the lightning bolt modelled as two congruent triangles ABC and DEF, sides 12 cm, 15 cm and 7 cm, with angle ABC marked α°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/043-the-save-my-exams-circular-logo-with-the-lightni.png)

Calculate the size of the angle $α ^{\circ}$, giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
$α ^{\circ}$ is angle $A B C$, opposite the side $A C = 7$, so rearrange the cosine rule for the angle

$\text{cos}  α ^{\circ} = \frac{12^{2}+15^{2}-7^{2}}{2(12)(15)} = \frac{320}{360}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine

`\alpha = \text{cos}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{320}{360}\right) = 27.266 \ldots°`

$α = 27 . 3 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement of the cosine rule for the angle, $\text{cos}  α ^{\circ} = \frac{12^{2}+15^{2}-7^{2}}{2(12)(15)}$.
> 
> **A1**: $α = 27 . 3 ^{\circ}$, to 1 decimal place (answers which round to $27 . 3 ^{\circ}$).

parts.problemMd: For the banner, the side lengths of the triangles are enlarged by a scale factor of $10$. Find the area the lightning bolt will take up on the banner, giving your answer in m².
parts.solutionMd:
The bolt is two congruent triangles, so find the area of one and double it

$\text{Area of bolt} = 2 \times \frac{1}{2} ( 12 ) ( 15 )  \text{sin}  27 . 3 ^{\circ} = 82 . 46 \dots \text{cm}^{2}$

**[M1]**

Enlarging lengths by scale factor $10$ multiplies areas by $10^{2} = 100$; then convert cm² to m² by dividing by $10  000$

$82 . 46 \dots \times 100 = 8246 \dots \text{cm}^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 0 . 825 \text{m}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct area of the lightning bolt as two triangles, $2 \times \frac{1}{2} ( 12 ) ( 15 )  \text{sin}  α ^{\circ}$ (answers which round to $82 . 5$ cm²).
> 
> **M1**: Applying the area scale factor $10^{2} = 100$ and converting to m² (dividing by $10  000$).
> 
> **A1**: Area $= 0 . 825$ m², correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:

Take the inverse sine, choosing the acute value

parts.problemMd: Show that the side length $B C$ is $9 . 43$ cm, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:

$B C$ is opposite the angle $B A C$, so use the cosine rule with the unrounded angle $B A C = 28 . 072 \dots ^{\circ}$ from part (a)

$B C^{2} = 10^{2} + 17^{2} - 2 ( 10 ) ( 17 )  \text{cos}  28 . 072 \dots ^{\circ} = 389 - 300 = 89$

**Final answer:** $B C = \sqrt{89} = 9 . 43$** cm**

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine

$B C A = \text{cos}^{-1} ( 0 . 8667 \dots ) = 29 . 924 \dots ^{\circ}$

$B C A = 29 . 9 ^{\circ}$

parts.problemMd: A point $D$ is placed on the side $A C$ so that $B D = B C$. Find the area of triangle $B C D$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

> **A1**: Area $= 38 . 5$ cm², correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the area of the field, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows triangle $P Q R$ with a point $S$ on $P R$. $P Q = 13$ cm, $Q R = 5 . 8$ cm, $Q S = y$ cm, angle $Q S P = 102 ^{\circ}$, angle $Q R S = 37 ^{\circ}$ and angle $Q P S = x ^{\circ}$.

![Triangle PQR with a line from Q to point S on PR; PQ = 13 cm, QR = 5.8 cm, QS = y cm, angle QSP = 102°, angle QRS = 37° and angle QPS = x°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/025-triangle-pqr-with-a-line-from-q-to-point-s-on-pr.png)

Calculate the values of $x$ and $y$, giving your answers to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $P S R$ is a straight line, angle $Q S R = 180 ^{\circ} - 102 ^{\circ} = 78 ^{\circ}$. Work in triangle $Q S R$, where $y = Q S$ is opposite the $37 ^{\circ}$ angle

$\frac{y}{\text{sin}37^{\circ}} = \frac{5.8}{\text{sin}78^{\circ}}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $y = 3 . 57$** cm**

**[A1]**

Now work in triangle $P Q S$, where $P Q = 13$ is opposite the $102 ^{\circ}$ angle and $Q S$ is opposite $x ^{\circ}$

$\frac{\text{sin}x^{\circ}}{3.5686\dots} = \frac{\text{sin}102^{\circ}}{13}$

$\text{sin}  x ^{\circ} = 0 . 2685 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine

$x = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 2685 \dots ) = 15 . 575 \dots ^{\circ}$

$x = 15 . 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for $y$ — using angle $Q S R = 78 ^{\circ}$ and the sine rule in triangle $Q S R$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $y = 3 . 57$ cm.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the sine rule in triangle $P Q S$ to find $x$ (using your $Q S$).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to $x = 15 . 6$.

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $A B C$ has $A B = 2 x$ cm, $B C = ( x + 5 )$ cm and $A C = 7$ cm. The angle $A B C = 60 ^{\circ}$.

Find the value of $x$, giving your answer as a simplified surd.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = 2x cm, BC = (x + 5) cm, AC = 7 cm and angle ABC = 60°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/029-triangle-abc-with-ab-2x-cm-bc-x-5-cm-ac-7-cm-and.png)

$A C$ is opposite the angle $B = 60 ^{\circ}$, so apply the cosine rule (with $\text{cos}  60 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$)

$7^{2} = ( 2 x )^{2} + ( x + 5 )^{2} - 2 ( 2 x ) ( x + 5 )  \text{cos}  60 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Expand and simplify — the term $2 ( 2 x ) ( x + 5 ) \times \frac{1}{2} = 2 x^{2} + 10 x$ cancels the linear terms

$49 = 5 x^{2} + 10 x + 25 - ( 2 x^{2} + 10 x ) = 3 x^{2} + 25$

**[A1]**

$3 x^{2} = 24 \Rightarrow x^{2} = 8$

$x = 2 \sqrt{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct cosine rule with the given expressions substituted and $\text{cos}  60 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplification to $3 x^{2} + 25 = 49$ (or $3 x^{2} = 24$).
> 
> **A1**: $x = 2 \sqrt{2}$ (a positive length; $\sqrt{8}$ simplified).

parts.problemMd: The area of the triangle can be written in the form $a \sqrt{6} + b \sqrt{3}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers. Find the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the area formula with the sides enclosing the $60 ^{\circ}$ angle and $x = 2 \sqrt{2}$

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 2 x ) ( x + 5 )  \text{sin}  60 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} ( 2 x ) ( x + 5 )$

**[M1]**

Expand the surd product with $x = 2 \sqrt{2}$

$( 2 x ) ( x + 5 ) = 4 \sqrt{2}  ( 2 \sqrt{2} + 5 ) = 16 + 20 \sqrt{2}$

**[M1]**

Multiply by $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ and compare with the form $a \sqrt{6} + b \sqrt{3}$

$\text{Area} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} ( 16 + 20 \sqrt{2} ) = 4 \sqrt{3} + 5 \sqrt{6}$

$a = 5 ,  b = 4$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula $\frac{1}{2} ( 2 x ) ( x + 5 )  \text{sin}  60 ^{\circ}$ with $x = 2 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $x = 2 \sqrt{2}$ and expanding the surd product to $16 + 20 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Area $= 4 \sqrt{3} + 5 \sqrt{6}$, giving $a = 5$ and $b = 4$.

parts.problemMd:
Two different triangles each have $A B = 2 . 8$ cm, $B C = 3 . 5$ cm and angle $A C B = 43 ^{\circ}$.

Find the largest angle in each of the triangles.
parts.solutionMd:
The information (two sides and a non-included angle) gives two possible triangles, shown together in the diagram below

![Combined ambiguous-case figure: apex B joined to the two positions of C on a base line, with BC = 3.5 cm and a 43° base angle at each C, and the shared side BA = 2.8 cm to point A between them; the angle at A is acute in one triangle and obtuse in the other.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/022-combined-ambiguous-case-figure-apex-b-joined-to-.png)

Angle $B A C$ is opposite $B C = 3 . 5$ and the $43 ^{\circ}$ angle is opposite $A B = 2 . 8$. Use the sine rule

$\frac{\text{sin}BAC}{3.5} = \frac{\text{sin}43^{\circ}}{2.8} \Rightarrow \text{sin}  B A C = 0 . 8525 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine to obtain the acute value

$B A C = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 8525 \dots ) = 58 . 484 \dots ^{\circ}$

The acute solution is $B A C = 58 . 5 ^{\circ}$, and by the symmetry of the sine graph the obtuse solution is

* *$180 ^{\circ} - 58 . 5 ^{\circ} = 121 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

In the triangle with the obtuse angle, $B A C = 121 . 5 ^{\circ}$ is already the largest angle

$\text{Largest angle} = 121 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

In the triangle with $B A C = 58 . 5 ^{\circ}$, the largest angle is $A B C = 180 ^{\circ} - 43 ^{\circ} - 58 . 5 ^{\circ}$

$\text{Largest angle} = 78 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the sine rule to find $\text{sin}  B A C$, for example $\frac{\text{sin}BAC}{3.5} = \frac{\text{sin}43^{\circ}}{2.8}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acute value $58 . 5 ^{\circ}$ (answers which round to $58 . 5 ^{\circ}$).
> 
> **A1**: Largest angle of the second triangle $= 121 . 5 ^{\circ}$, found from $180 ^{\circ} - 58 . 5 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Largest angle of the first triangle $= 78 . 5 ^{\circ}$ (angle $A B C$).

parts.problemMd:
A triangular field has an area of $157$ m². Two of its side lengths are $13 . 2$ m and $28 . 4$ m, and the angle $θ$ lies between these two sides.

Find the two possible values of $θ$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle with two sides 13.2 m and 28.4 m enclosing the angle θ; the triangle has an area of 157 m².](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/028-triangle-with-two-sides-13-2-m-and-28-4-m-enclos.png)

The angle $θ$ is between the two known sides, so use the area formula

$\frac{1}{2} ( 13 . 2 ) ( 28 . 4 )  \text{sin}  θ = 157$

**[M1]**

$\text{sin}  θ = \frac{157}{187.44} = 0 . 8376 \dots$

**[A1]**

Take the inverse sine to obtain the acute value

$θ = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 8376 \dots ) = 56 . 888 \dots ^{\circ}$

By the symmetry of the sine graph, $\text{sin}  θ = \text{sin}  ( 180 ^{\circ} - θ )$ also gives an obtuse solution

**Final answer:** $θ = 56 . 9 ^{\circ}$** or **$θ = 123 . 1 ^{\circ}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula equated to $157$, $\frac{1}{2} ( 13 . 2 ) ( 28 . 4 )  \text{sin}  θ = 157$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $\text{sin}  θ = 0 . 838$ (answers which round to $0 . 838$).
> 
> **A1**: Acute value $θ = 56 . 9 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Obtuse value $θ = 123 . 1 ^{\circ}$, from $180 ^{\circ} - 56 . 9 ^{\circ}$.

parts.problemMd: Given that $θ$ is acute, calculate the perimeter of the field, giving your answer to the nearest metre.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $θ = 56 . 9 ^{\circ}$. The third side is opposite $θ$, so apply the cosine rule

$c^{2} = 13 . 2^{2} + 28 . 4^{2} - 2 ( 13 . 2 ) ( 28 . 4 )  \text{cos}  56 . 9 ^{\circ}$

$c^{2} = 571 . 4 \dots \Rightarrow c = 23 . 9 \dots$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the three sides

$P = 13 . 2 + 28 . 4 + 23 . 9 \dots = 65 . 5 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 66$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the cosine rule for the third side, $c^{2} = 13 . 2^{2} + 28 . 4^{2} - 2 ( 13 . 2 ) ( 28 . 4 )  \text{cos}  56 . 9 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct third side (answers which round to $23 . 9$ m).
> 
> **A1**: Perimeter $= 66$ m, to the nearest metre.

parts.problemMd: Given that $B C = 1$ inch, use the angles from parts (a) and (b) (correct to 1 decimal place) to calculate the area of the quadrilateral $A B C D$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with the diagonal AC drawn and equal sides AB = CD marked; the ratio side lengths AB = 2, BC = 4 and AC = 5 are shown, together with the angles found in parts (a) and (b): ABC = 108.2°, CAD = 22.3° and ADC = 71.8°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/032-cyclic-quadrilateral-abcd-with-the-diagonal-ac-d.png)

The ratio value of $B C$ is $4$, so with $B C = 1$ inch, divide every length by $4$

$A B = C D = 0 . 5 ,  A C = 1 . 25  ( \text{inches} )$

**[M1]**

The diagonal $A C$ splits $A B C D$ into triangles $A B C$ and $A C D$. In triangle $A C D$, the angles $A D C = 71 . 8 ^{\circ}$ and $C A D = 22 . 3 ^{\circ}$ were found in part (b), so the third angle is

$A C D = 180 ^{\circ} - 71 . 8 ^{\circ} - 22 . 3 ^{\circ} = 85 . 9 ^{\circ}$

Add the areas of the two triangles, each using $\frac{1}{2} a b  \text{sin}  C$

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 0 . 5 ) ( 1 )  \text{sin}  108 . 2 ^{\circ} + \frac{1}{2} ( 1 . 25 ) ( 0 . 5 )  \text{sin}  85 . 9 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 0 . 549 \text{inches}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct side lengths from $B C = 1$ inch (dividing the ratio values by $4$).
> 
> **M1**: Correct method — area of triangle $A B C$ plus area of triangle $A C D$, each using $\frac{1}{2} a b  \text{sin}  C$, with $A C D = 85 . 9 ^{\circ}$ found from the part (b) angles ($71 . 8 ^{\circ}$ and $22 . 3 ^{\circ}$).
> 
> **A1**: Area $= 0 . 549$ inches², correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
In triangle $A B C$, $A B = 2 x$ cm, $B C = 10$ cm and $A C = ( 20 - 2 x )$ cm. Angle $A B C = θ$.

Show that $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{4x-15}{2x}$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = 2x cm, BC = 10 cm, AC = (20 - 2x) cm and angle ABC = θ.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/020-triangle-abc-with-ab-2x-cm-bc-10-cm-ac-20-2x-cm-.png)

$A C$ is opposite the angle $B = θ$, so apply the cosine rule

$( 20 - 2 x )^{2} = ( 2 x )^{2} + 10^{2} - 2 ( 2 x ) ( 10 )  \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Expand: $400 - 80 x + 4 x^{2} = 4 x^{2} + 100 - 40 x  \text{cos}  θ$. The $4 x^{2}$ cancels, so $40 x  \text{cos}  θ = 80 x - 300$

**Final answer:** $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{80x-300}{40x} = \frac{4x-15}{2x}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct cosine rule with the given expressions substituted, $( 20 - 2 x )^{2} = ( 2 x )^{2} + 10^{2} - 2 ( 2 x ) ( 10 )  \text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct expansion and rearrangement to the printed result $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{4x-15}{2x}$.

parts.problemMd: Given that $\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$, find the area of the triangle.
parts.solutionMd:
Set the expression from part (a) equal to $- \frac{1}{2}$ and solve for $x$

$\frac{4x-15}{2x} = - \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow 8 x - 30 = - 2 x \Rightarrow 10 x = 30$

**[M1]**

$x = 3 \Rightarrow A B = 6 ,  B C = 10$

**[A1]**

Since $\text{cos}  θ = - \frac{1}{2}$, take the inverse cosine

`\theta = \text{cos}^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 120°`

Use the area formula with the two sides enclosing $θ$

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 6 ) ( 10 )  \text{sin}  120 ^{\circ} = 30 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 15 \sqrt{3} \text{cm}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $\frac{4x-15}{2x} = - \frac{1}{2}$ and solving for $x$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = 3$, giving $A B = 6$ and $B C = 10$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula with $\text{sin}  120 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Area $= 15 \sqrt{3}$ cm² (accept $26 . 0$ cm² to 3 significant figures).

parts.problemMd:
An artist is designing a triangular sculpture, made using three equal lengths of metal piping. When laid flat, the sculpture covers $21 . 8$ m².

Calculate the total length of metal piping needed. Give your answer to the nearest cm.
parts.solutionMd:
![Equilateral triangle with three equal sides marked by tick marks.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/021-equilateral-triangle-with-three-equal-sides-mark.png)

Three equal lengths make an equilateral triangle of side $s$, with a $60 ^{\circ}$ angle between each pair of sides. Use the area formula

$\frac{1}{2} s^{2}  \text{sin}  60 ^{\circ} = 21 . 8$

**[M1]**

$s^{2} = \frac{21.8}{\frac{1}{2}\text{sin}60^{\circ}} = 50 . 34 \dots$

**[A1]**

$s = 7 . 095 \dots$* m*

**[A1]**

The total piping is the perimeter, $3 s$; convert metres to centimetres

$3 s = 21 . 286 \dots \text{m} = 2128 . 6 \dots \text{cm}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $2129$** cm**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula for an equilateral triangle equated to $21 . 8$, for example $\frac{1}{2} s^{2}  \text{sin}  60 ^{\circ} = 21 . 8$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $s^{2}$ (answers which round to $50 . 3$).
> 
> **A1**: Side length $s = 7 . 10$ m (answers which round to $7 . 095$).
> 
> **M1**: Finding the perimeter $3 s$ and converting to centimetres.
> 
> **A1**: $2129$ cm, to the nearest cm. Allow 21.29 m.

parts.problemMd:
An isosceles triangle has two of its side lengths equal to $7 . 3$ cm and $9 . 8$ cm.

Calculate the difference between the two possible smallest angles.
parts.solutionMd:
Because the triangle is isosceles, either the $7 . 3$ cm or the $9 . 8$ cm side is repeated, giving two possible triangles. In each, the smallest angle is opposite the shortest side.

![Triangle 1: isosceles triangle with sides 9.8 cm, 9.8 cm and 7.3 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/017-triangle-1-isosceles-triangle-with-sides-9-8-cm-.png)

![Triangle 2: isosceles triangle with sides 7.3 cm, 7.3 cm and 9.8 cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/018-triangle-2-isosceles-triangle-with-sides-7-3-cm-.png)

For the triangle with sides $7 . 3$, $7 . 3$, $9 . 8$, the smallest angle is a base angle. Find the apex (opposite $9 . 8$) first

$\text{cos} θ = \frac{7.3^{2}+7.3^{2}-9.8^{2}}{2(7.3)(7.3)} = 0 . 0989 \dots$

Take the inverse cosine

$θ=\text{cos}^{-1}(0.0989\dots)=84.325\dots$

$\text{smallest angle}=\frac{180\circ-84.325\dots\circ}{2}=47.838\dots$

**[M1 A1]**

For the triangle with sides $9 . 8$, $9 . 8$, $7 . 3$, the smallest angle is opposite the $7 . 3$ side

$\text{cos} θ = \frac{9.8^{2}+9.8^{2}-7.3^{2}}{2(9.8)(9.8)} = 0 . 7225 \dots$

Take the inverse cosine

$θ=\text{cos}^{-1}(0.7225\dots)=43.733\dots$

**[A1]**

Subtract the two smallest angles to find the difference

$\text{Difference}=47.838\dots-43.733\dots=4.10^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising the two possible isosceles triangles and using the cosine rule to find a smallest angle in one of them.
> 
> **A1**: Smallest angle of the $7 . 3 , 7 . 3 , 9 . 8$ triangle $=47.8^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Smallest angle of the $9 . 8 , 9 . 8 , 7 . 3$ triangle $=43.7^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Difference $=4.10^{\circ}$ (answers which round to $4.1^{\circ}$).

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $A B C$ has $A B = 3 x$ cm, $B C = 5 x$ cm and $A C = 6 x$ cm.

Calculate the size of angle $B A C$, giving your answer to 2 decimal places.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with sides 3x cm, 5x cm and 6x cm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/016-triangle-abc-with-sides-3x-cm-5x-cm-and-6x-cm.png)

$B A C$ is opposite $B C = 5 x$. Rearranging the cosine rule, the $x^{2}$ terms cancel

$\text{cos}  B A C = \frac{(3x)^{2}+(6x)^{2}-(5x)^{2}}{2(3x)(6x)} = \frac{20x^{2}}{36x^{2}} = \frac{5}{9}$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse cosine

`BAC = \text{cos}^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right) = 56.251 \ldots°`

$B A C = 56 . 25 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement of the cosine rule with the $x$ terms cancelling, $\text{cos}  B A C = \frac{(3x)^{2}+(6x)^{2}-(5x)^{2}}{2(3x)(6x)}$.
> 
> **A1**: $B A C = 56 . 25 ^{\circ}$, to 2 decimal places.

parts.problemMd: Given that the perimeter of the triangle is $37 . 8$ cm, find the area of the triangle, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The perimeter is $3 x + 5 x + 6 x = 14 x$

$14 x = 37 . 8 \Rightarrow x = 2 . 7$

**[M1]**

So $A B = 8 . 1$, $B C = 13 . 5$ and $A C = 16 . 2$ cm

**[A1]**

Use the area formula with the two sides enclosing angle $B A C$

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 8 . 1 ) ( 16 . 2 )  \text{sin}  56 . 25 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 54 . 6 \text{cm}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Using $14 x = 37 . 8$ to find $x = 2 . 7$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct side lengths, $8 . 1$, $13 . 5$ and $16 . 2$ cm.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula (or Heron's formula) with the side lengths.
> 
> **A1**: Area $= 54 . 6$ cm², correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.problemMd:
Triangles $P S Q$ and $S Q R$ are such that $P S = S Q = Q R$, where $S$ lies on $P R$. $P Q = 15$ cm, $Q R = 2 x$ cm and angle $P S Q = 120 ^{\circ}$.

![Triangle PQR with S on PR and QS drawn; PS = SQ = QR (equal tick marks), PQ = 15 cm, QR = 2x cm and angle PSQ = 120°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/014-triangle-pqr-with-s-on-pr-and-qs-drawn-ps-sq-qr-.png)

Calculate the exact value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle PQR with QS to point S on PR; PS = SQ = QR (equal tick marks); PQ = 15 cm, QR = 2x cm, angle PSQ = 120°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/015-triangle-pqr-with-qs-to-point-s-on-pr-ps-sq-qr-e.png)

In triangle $P S Q$, $P S = S Q$, so it is isosceles with apex angle $P S Q = 120 ^{\circ}$. The base angles are equal

$\text{angle} S P Q = \text{angle} P Q S = \frac{180^{\circ}-120^{\circ}}{2} = 30 ^{\circ}$

Apply the sine rule, with $S Q = 2 x$ opposite the $30 ^{\circ}$ angle and $P Q = 15$ opposite the $120 ^{\circ}$ angle

$\frac{2x}{\text{sin}30^{\circ}} = \frac{15}{\text{sin}120^{\circ}}$

**[M1]**

$2 x = \frac{15\text{sin}30^{\circ}}{\text{sin}120^{\circ}} = 5 \sqrt{3}$

**[A1]**

$x = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Finding the base angle $30 ^{\circ}$ and setting up the sine rule, $\frac{2x}{\text{sin}30^{\circ}} = \frac{15}{\text{sin}120^{\circ}}$.
> 
> **A1**: $2 x = 5 \sqrt{3}$ (exact).
> 
> **A1**: $x = \frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the area of triangle $P Q R$, leaving your answer in surd form.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle PQR with QS to point S on PR; PS = SQ = QR (equal tick marks); PQ = 15 cm, QR = 2x cm, angle PSQ = 120°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/015-triangle-pqr-with-qs-to-point-s-on-pr-ps-sq-qr-e.png)

Angle $Q S R = 180 ^{\circ} - 120 ^{\circ} = 60 ^{\circ}$. In triangle $S Q R$, $S Q = Q R$ with a base angle of $60 ^{\circ}$, so it is equilateral and angle $S Q R = 60 ^{\circ}$. Therefore

$\text{angle} P Q R = \text{angle} P Q S + \text{angle} S Q R = 30 ^{\circ} + 60 ^{\circ} = 90 ^{\circ}$

Triangle $P Q R$ is right-angled at $Q$, so its area is half the product of the two legs $P Q$ and $Q R = 2 x = 5 \sqrt{3}$

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 15 ) ( 5 \sqrt{3} )$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = \frac{75\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{cm}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Recognising angle $P Q R = 90 ^{\circ}$ (or using the area formula) with $P Q = 15$ and $Q R = 5 \sqrt{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Area $= \frac{75\sqrt{3}}{2}$ cm² (accept $37 . 5 \sqrt{3}$ cm²).

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a field $A B C D$ in which unicorns are kept, where $A B$ is parallel to $C D$. $A B = 318$ m, $C D = 235$ m, $A D = 142$ m and angle $D A B = 92 ^{\circ}$.

![Trapezium field ABCD with AB parallel to CD (same-direction arrows); AB = 318 m, CD = 235 m, AD = 142 m and angle DAB = 92°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/011-trapezium-field-abcd-with-ab-parallel-to-cd-same.png)

To be happy, each unicorn needs at least $2222$ m² of the field. Calculate the maximum number of unicorns that can happily be kept in the field.
parts.solutionMd:
![Trapezium field ABCD with AB parallel to CD (AB = 318 m, CD = 235 m, AD = 142 m, angle DAB = 92°), split by the diagonal BD into triangles ABD and BDC.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/012-trapezium-field-abcd-with-ab-parallel-to-cd-ab-3.png)

Draw the diagonal $B D$. In triangle $A B D$ the angle $D A B = 92 ^{\circ}$ is known, so find $B D$ with the cosine rule

$B D^{2} = 142^{2} + 318^{2} - 2 ( 142 ) ( 318 )  \text{cos}  92 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$B D = 352 . 76 \dots$* m*

**[A1]**

Find angle $A B D$ with the sine rule (needed for the second triangle)

$\text{sin}  A B D = \frac{142\text{sin}92^{\circ}}{352.76\dots} = 0 . 4022 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take the inverse sine

$A B D = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 4022 \dots ) = 23 . 722 \dots ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Since $A B$ is parallel to $C D$, angle $B D C =$ angle $A B D = 23 . 72 ^{\circ}$ (alternate angles), so the area of the field is the sum of the two triangles

$\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 142 ) ( 318 )  \text{sin}  92 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$+  \frac{1}{2} ( 235 ) ( 352 . 76 )  \text{sin}  23 . 72 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Area} = 22564 + 16674 = 39238 \dots \text{m}^{2}$

**[A1]**

Divide by the area each unicorn needs, then round down

$\frac{39238\dots}{2222} = 17 . 6 \dots$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $17$** unicorns**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the cosine rule in triangle $A B D$ for the diagonal $B D$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct diagonal (answers which round to $353$ m).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the sine rule to find angle $A B D$.
> 
> **A1**: Angle $A B D = 23 . 7 ^{\circ}$ (answers which round to $23 . 7 ^{\circ}$).
> 
> **M1**: Correct area of triangle $A B D$, $\frac{1}{2} ( 142 ) ( 318 )  \text{sin}  92 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct area of triangle $B D C$, using angle $B D C = 23 . 72 ^{\circ}$ from alternate angles.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total area (answers which round to $39200$ m²).
> 
> **M1**: Dividing the total area by $2222$.
> 
> **A1**: $17$ unicorns, having rounded down to a whole number.

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $A B C$ has $A B = x$ cm, $B C = ( 4 - x )$ cm, angle $B A C = θ$ and angle $B C A = 30 ^{\circ}$.

Given that $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, show that $x = 4 ( \sqrt{2} - 1 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = x cm, BC = (4 - x) cm, angle BAC = θ and angle BCA = 30°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/019-triangle-abc-with-ab-x-cm-bc-4-x-cm-angle-bac-an.png)

$B C$ is opposite $θ$ and $A B$ is opposite the $30 ^{\circ}$ angle, so use the sine rule

$\frac{4-x}{\text{sin}θ} = \frac{x}{\text{sin}30^{\circ}}$

**[M1]**

Substitute $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$

$( 4 - x ) \sqrt{2} = 2 x$

**[A1]**

Collect the terms in $x$

$4 \sqrt{2} = 2 x + x \sqrt{2} = x ( 2 + \sqrt{2} )$

**[M1]**

$x = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}$

**[A1]**

Rationalise by multiplying by $\frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2-\sqrt{2}}$

$x = \frac{4\sqrt{2}(2-\sqrt{2})}{4-2} = 2 \sqrt{2}  ( 2 - \sqrt{2} ) = 4 \sqrt{2} - 4$

**Final answer:** $x = 4 ( \sqrt{2} - 1 )$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the sine rule, $\frac{4-x}{\text{sin}θ} = \frac{x}{\text{sin}30^{\circ}}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation after substituting the exact sines, $( 4 - x ) \sqrt{2} = 2 x$.
> 
> **M1**: Collecting the $x$ terms, $x ( 2 + \sqrt{2} ) = 4 \sqrt{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $x = \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}$.
> 
> **A1**: Rationalising to reach the printed result $x = 4 ( \sqrt{2} - 1 )$.

parts.problemMd:
Triangle $A B C$ has $A B = 3 x$ cm, $A C = ( x + 5 )$ cm and angle $B A C = 150 ^{\circ}$. The area of the triangle is $7 \frac{1}{4}$ cm².

Find the ratio of the angles of the triangle, to the nearest degree, in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
![Triangle ABC with AB = 3x cm and AC = (x + 5) cm enclosing the angle 150°.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/basic-trigonometry/assets/013-triangle-abc-with-ab-3x-cm-and-ac-x-5-cm-enclosi.png)

Use the area formula with $\text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$ to form an equation in $x$

$\frac{1}{2} ( 3 x ) ( x + 5 )  \text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = 7 \frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \frac{3x^{2}+15x}{4} = \frac{29}{4}$

**[M1]**

$3 x^{2} + 15 x - 29 = 0$

**[A1]**

Solve with the quadratic formula, taking the positive root

$x = \frac{-15+\sqrt{573}}{6} = 1 . 489 \dots \Rightarrow A B = 4 . 468 ,  A C = 6 . 489$

**[M1]**

Find the third side $B C$ with the cosine rule

$B C^{2} = 4 . 468^{2} + 6 . 489^{2} - 2 ( 4 . 468 ) ( 6 . 489 )  \text{cos}  150 ^{\circ} = 112 . 3 \dots \Rightarrow B C = 10 . 60 \dots$

**[M1]**

Find angle $C$ (opposite $A B$) with the sine rule; then $B = 180 ^{\circ} - 150 ^{\circ} - C$

$\text{sin}  C = \frac{4.468\text{sin}150^{\circ}}{10.60} = 0 . 2108$

Take the inverse sine

$C = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 2108 ) = 12 . 171 \dots ^{\circ} \approx 12 ^{\circ}$

$B = 180 ^{\circ} - 150 ^{\circ} - 12 . 171 \dots ^{\circ} = 17 . 829 \dots ^{\circ} \approx 18 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

The angles are $150 ^{\circ}$, $18 ^{\circ}$ and $12 ^{\circ}$; divide the ratio by $6$

$A : B : C = 25 : 3 : 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the area formula with $\text{sin}  150 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$, equated to $7 \frac{1}{4}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic $3 x^{2} + 15 x - 29 = 0$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the quadratic for the positive value of $x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the cosine rule for $B C$.
> 
> **A1**: All three angles correct to the nearest degree, $150 ^{\circ}$, $18 ^{\circ}$ and $12 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Ratio $25 : 3 : 2$ in its simplest form.

parts.problemMd:
Without using a calculator, write down:

(i) $60 ^{\circ}$ in radians

(ii) $\text{sin}  45 ^{\circ}$

(iii) $\text{tan}  π$

(iv) $\frac{5π}{6}$ radians in degrees

(v) $\text{cos}  0$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Convert using $180 ^{\circ} = π$ radians, so multiply the degrees by $\frac{π}{180}$

$60 ^{\circ} = 60 \times \frac{π}{180}$

$\frac{π}{3}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

$\text{sin}  45 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

$\text{tan}  π = 0$

**[B1]**

(iv)

Convert using $π \text{radians} = 180 ^{\circ}$, so multiply by $\frac{180^{\circ}}{π}$

$\frac{5π}{6} = \frac{5π}{6} \times \frac{180^{\circ}}{π}$

$150 ^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

(v)

$\text{cos}  0 = 1$

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
A quarter circle is a sector with a right angle at the centre, so its area is a quarter of the whole circle

Divide both sides by $π$ and multiply by 4

$r^{2} = 72$

Take the positive square root, since a radius must be positive

$r = 6 \sqrt{2} \text{cm}$

**Final answer:** $\text{Area} = \frac{π}{6} ( p + 8 )^{2} \text{cm}^{2}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Radius $O A = O B = p + 8$ (from $O C = 8$ and $C B = p$), used in $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $θ = \frac{π}{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correctly simplified to the printed $\frac{π}{6} ( p + 8 )^{2}$ cm².

parts.problemMd: Show that the area of the triangle $O C D$ is $16 \sqrt{3}$ cm².
parts.solutionMd:
![Circle sector OAB, centre O at the right vertex, centre angle pi/3; A and B lie on the arc; D lies on OA and C lies on OB with OD = OC = 8 cm and AD = BC = p cm; the chord AB and the parallel line CD are both drawn; the region ABCD, the sector minus triangle OCD, is shaded; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/019-circle-sector-oab-centre-o-at-the-right-vertex-c.png)

The triangle $O C D$ has $O C = O D = 8$ enclosing the angle $\frac{π}{3}$, so use $\frac{1}{2} a b  \text{sin}  C$ with the exact value $\text{sin} \frac{π}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

`\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}(8)(8)\,\text{sin}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 32 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}`

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Area} = 16 \sqrt{3} \text{cm}^{2}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $\frac{1}{2} a b  \text{sin}  C$ with $a = b = 8$ and $C = \frac{π}{3}$, using the exact value $\text{sin} \frac{π}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correctly reaches the printed $16 \sqrt{3}$ cm².

parts.problemMd: Given that the area of the shaded shape $A B C D$ is `\left(\dfrac{50\pi}{3} - 16\sqrt{3}\right)` cm², find the value of $p$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Circle sector OAB, centre O at the right vertex, centre angle pi/3; A and B lie on the arc; D lies on OA and C lies on OB with OD = OC = 8 cm and AD = BC = p cm; the chord AB and the parallel line CD are both drawn; the region ABCD, the sector minus triangle OCD, is shaded; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/019-circle-sector-oab-centre-o-at-the-right-vertex-c.png)

The shaded shape $A B C D$ is the sector $O A B$ with the triangle $O C D$ removed. Set this equal to the given area

$\frac{π}{6} ( p + 8 )^{2} - 16 \sqrt{3} = \frac{50π}{3} - 16 \sqrt{3}$

**[M1]**

The $16 \sqrt{3}$ terms cancel, leaving

$\frac{π}{6} ( p + 8 )^{2} = \frac{50π}{3}$

Multiply both sides by $\frac{6}{π}$ to solve for $( p + 8 )^{2}$

$( p + 8 )^{2} = 100$

**[A1]**

Take the square root of both sides

$p + 8 = \pm 10$

**[M1]**

Since $p$ is a length it must be positive, so reject the negative root

$p = 2 \text{cm}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Shaded $A B C D =$ sector $O A B -$ triangle $O C D$, equated to the given area $\frac{50π}{3} - 16 \sqrt{3}$.
> 
> **A1**: $( p + 8 )^{2} = 100$ (after the $16 \sqrt{3}$ terms cancel).
> 
> **M1**: Square-rooting to $p + 8 = \pm 10$.
> 
> **A1**: $p = 2$ cm, rejecting $p = - 18$ because $p$ is a length.

parts.problemMd:
A sector of a circle has area $8 π$ cm² and arc length $4 π$ cm.

![A sector of a circle, centre O, with arc length 4 pi cm, radius r cm and area 8 pi cm squared; the angle theta at the centre is to be found](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/001-a-sector-of-a-circle-centre-o-with-arc-length-4-.png)

Find the radius of the circle and the angle at the centre of the sector.
parts.solutionMd:
Set up an equation for the area and an equation for the arc length, using $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ and $s = r θ$

$\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ = 8 π$

$r θ = 4 π$

**[M1]**

Make $θ$ the subject of the arc-length equation, then substitute it into the area equation to eliminate $θ$

$θ = \frac{4π}{r}$

`\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{r}\right) = 8\pi`

$2 π r = 8 π$

$r = 4 \text{cm}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $r = 4$ back into the arc-length equation to find the angle

$4 θ = 4 π$

**[M1]**

$θ = π \text{radians}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Two correct equations set up — area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ = 8 π$ and arc $r θ = 4 π$.
> 
> **A1**: $r = 4$ cm, found by eliminating $θ$ (for example substituting $θ = \frac{4π}{r}$, or dividing the two equations).
> 
> **M1**: Substitute your radius back into $r θ = 4 π$ (or $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ = 8 π$) to find the angle.
> 
> **A1**: $θ = π$ radians.

parts.problemMd:
The canopy of a parachute and the two outermost suspension lines form a sector of a circle $O A B$, as shown below, with the parachutist modelled as a particle at the point $O$.

![Sector OAB representing a parachute: centre O at the bottom vertex, the two outermost suspension lines OA and OB of length r as the radii, the angle AOB equal to theta, the chord AB drawn, and the canopy shown as the shaded region above AB; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/006-sector-oab-representing-a-parachute-centre-o-at-.png)

The area of the sector $O A B$ is $\frac{125π}{144}$ m², and the length of the arc $A B$ is $\frac{25π}{36}$ m.

Find the length of one suspension line, and the angle $A O B$ that the two outermost suspension lines make at the parachutist.
parts.solutionMd:
Each suspension line is a radius $r$, and the angle $A O B$ is $θ$. Write the arc length and the area in terms of $r$ and $θ$

$r θ = \frac{25π}{36}$

$\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ = \frac{125π}{144}$

**[M1]**

Double the area equation to give $r^{2} θ = \frac{125π}{72}$, then divide it by the arc equation; the $θ$ cancels, leaving $r$

$r = \frac{r^{2}θ}{rθ} = \frac{125π/72}{25π/36}$

**[M1]**

$r = \frac{5}{2} \text{m}$

**[A1]**

Substitute back into the arc equation to find the angle

$θ = \frac{25π/36}{r} = \frac{25π/36}{5/2}$

**[M1]**

$θ = \frac{5π}{18} \text{radians}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both relationships set up — arc $r θ = \frac{25π}{36}$ and area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ = \frac{125π}{144}$.
> 
> **M1**: Dividing the (doubled) area equation by the arc equation to eliminate $θ$ and find $r$.
> 
> **A1**: $r = \frac{5}{2}$ m (that is 2.5 m).
> 
> **M1**: Substituting your $r$ into $r θ = \frac{25π}{36}$ to find $θ$.
> 
> **A1**: $θ = \frac{5π}{18}$ radians.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle $O A B$ with centre $O$, radius $r$ cm and angle $θ$ radians at the centre.

![Sector OAB of a circle, centre O; radii OA and OB each r cm, angle AOB = theta radians; the chord AB is drawn and the segment between chord AB and the arc is shaded; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/009-sector-oab-of-a-circle-centre-o-radii-oa-and-ob-.png)

Show that the area of the shaded segment is $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} ( θ - \text{sin}  θ )$ cm².
parts.solutionMd:
The shaded segment is the sector $O A B$ with the triangle $O A B$ removed

$\text{Segment} = \text{sector} - \text{triangle}$

**[M1]**

The sector has area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$, and the triangle has two sides $r$ enclosing $θ$, so its area is $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin}  θ$

$= \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ - \frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin}  θ$

**[M1]**

Factor out $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}$

**Final answer:** $= \frac{1}{2} r^{2} ( θ - \text{sin}  θ ) \text{cm}^{2}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Shaded segment formed as sector $-$ triangle.
> 
> **M1**: Sector area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ and triangle area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin}  θ$ both substituted.
> 
> **A1**: Factorised to the printed $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} ( θ - \text{sin}  θ )$.

parts.problemMd: Find, in terms of $θ$, the percentage of the sector that the segment occupies.
parts.solutionMd:
The percentage is the segment as a fraction of the sector, multiplied by 100

$\frac{\text{segment}}{\text{sector}} \times 100 = \frac{\frac{1}{2}r^{2}(θ-\text{sin}θ)}{\frac{1}{2}r^{2}θ} \times 100$

**[M1]**

The factor $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}$ cancels, leaving

`\dfrac{100(\theta - \text{sin}\,\theta)}{\theta}\%`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Percentage formed as $\frac{\text{segment}}{\text{sector}} \times 100$.
> 
> **A1**: `\dfrac{100(\theta - \text{sin}\,\theta)}{\theta}\%`, or equivalent such as `100\left(1 - \dfrac{\text{sin}\,\theta}{\theta}\right)\%`.

parts.problemMd:
The canopy of a parachute and the two outermost suspension lines form a sector of a circle, as shown below, with the parachutist modelled as a particle at the point $O$. The angle at the centre $O$ is $\frac{π}{3}$ radians.

![Sector OAB representing a parachute: centre O at the bottom vertex, the two outermost suspension lines OA and OB of length r as the radii, the angle at O equal to pi/3 radians, the chord AB drawn, and the canopy shown as the shaded region above AB; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/014-sector-oab-representing-a-parachute-centre-o-at-.png)

The area of the sector $O A B$ is $\frac{49π}{150}$ m².

The parachute is made with 40 equal-length suspension lines. Disregarding any extra cord needed for knots and fastenings, find the total length of suspension line required to make the parachute.
parts.solutionMd:
Each suspension line is a radius $r$ of the sector. Use $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $θ = \frac{π}{3}$ and the given area to find $r$

`\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{49\pi}{150}`

**[M1]**

Divide by $π$ and rearrange, then take the positive root

$r^{2} = \frac{49}{25}$

$r = \frac{7}{5} \text{m}$

**[A1]**

There are 40 equal lines, each of length $r$, so the total length is

$40 \times \frac{7}{5}$

**[M1]**

$= 56 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $θ = \frac{π}{3}$ and area $\frac{49π}{150}$, giving `\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{49\pi}{150}`.
> 
> **A1**: $r = \frac{7}{5}$ m (that is 1.4 m).
> 
> **M1**: Total length formed as 40 × your radius.
> 
> **A1**: Total length $= 56$ m.

parts.problemMd:
A sector of a circle $O P Q$ has radius $a$ cm, and the angle at the centre $O$ is $\frac{a}{3}$ radians.

![Sector OPQ of a circle, centre O at the vertex, with radii OP and OQ each of length a and the angle POQ at the centre equal to a over 3 radians, and arc PQ; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/011-sector-opq-of-a-circle-centre-o-at-the-vertex-wi.png)

Given that the area of the sector $O P Q$ (in cm²) is three times the length of the arc $P Q$ (in cm), find the value of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
Write the area and the arc in terms of $a$, using $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ and $s = r θ$ with $r = a$ and $θ = \frac{a}{3}$. The condition "area is three times the arc" gives

`\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \left(\frac{a}{3}\right) = 3 \times a \left(\frac{a}{3}\right)`

**[M1]**

Simplify each side

$\frac{a^{3}}{6} = a^{2}$

$a^{3} = 6 a^{2}$

**[A1]**

Bring everything to one side and factor out $a^{2}$

$a^{3} - 6 a^{2} = 0$

`a^{2} \left(a - 6\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Since $a$ is a radius it must be positive, so reject $a = 0$

$a = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Area and arc written in terms of $a$ with the condition area = 3 × arc, giving `\frac{1}{2} a^{2} \left(\frac{a}{3}\right) = 3 a \left(\frac{a}{3}\right)`.
> 
> **A1**: Simplified to $a^{3} = 6 a^{2}$ (or $\frac{a^{3}}{6} = a^{2}$).
> 
> **M1**: Factorised to `a^{2} \left(a - 6\right) = 0`.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 6$, rejecting $a = 0$ since $a$ is a radius.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle $O A B$ with centre $O$ and radius $r$ cm. The angle at the centre is 0.8 radians.

![Sector OAB of a circle, centre O; radii OA and OB each r cm, angle AOB = 0.8 radians; the chord AB is drawn and the segment between chord AB and the arc is shaded; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/012-sector-oab-of-a-circle-centre-o-radii-oa-and-ob-.png)

Given that the area of the triangle $O A B$ is 5.64 cm², find the area of the shaded segment, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The triangle $O A B$ has two sides of length $r$ enclosing the 0.8 rad angle, so its area is $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin} ( 0 . 8 )$. Set this equal to the given area to find $r^{2}$

$\frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin} ( 0 . 8 ) = 5 . 64$

**[M1]**

$r^{2} = \frac{2\times5.64}{\text{sin}(0.8)} = 15 . 7244 \dots$

**[A1]**

The shaded segment is the sector with the triangle removed. Find the sector area using $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$

$\text{Sector} = \frac{1}{2} ( 15 . 7244 \dots ) ( 0 . 8 ) = 6 . 2898 \dots$

**[M1]**

Subtract the triangle, keeping the unrounded values

$\text{Segment} = 6 . 2898 \dots - 5 . 64$

**[M1]**

$\text{Segment} = 0 . 650 \text{cm}^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Triangle area formed as $\frac{1}{2} r^{2}  \text{sin} ( 0 . 8 ) = 5 . 64$ to find $r^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $r^{2} = 15 . 7$ (answers which round to 15.7).
> 
> **M1**: Sector area using $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $θ = 0 . 8$.
> 
> **M1**: Shaded segment formed as sector area $-$ triangle area.
> 
> **A1**: Segment which rounds to 0.650 cm². Use the unrounded $r^{2}$ throughout.

parts.problemMd: Find the perimeter of the sector $O A B$, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The perimeter of the sector is the two radii plus the arc. Take $r = \sqrt{15.7244\dots} = 3 . 9654 \dots$ and find the arc with $s = r θ$

$s = r θ = 3 . 9654 \dots \times 0 . 8 = 3 . 1723 \dots$

**[M1]**

Add the two radii to the arc

$\text{Perimeter} = 2 r + s = 2 ( 3 . 9654 \dots ) + 3 . 1723 \dots$

**[M1]**

$\text{Perimeter} = 11 . 1 \text{cm}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: $r = \sqrt{\text{your}r^{2}} \approx 3 . 97$ and arc $= r θ$ with $θ = 0 . 8$.
> 
> **M1**: Perimeter formed as $2 r +$ arc.
> 
> **A1**: Perimeter which rounds to 11.1 cm.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a prism whose cross-section is a sector of a circle. The sector has radius $( 2 a - 3 )$ cm and the angle at the centre is 1.7 radians. The prism is 4 cm thick.

![A prism whose cross-section is a sector of a circle of radius (2a minus 3) cm with a centre angle of 1.7 radians, extruded to a thickness of 4 cm; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/013-a-prism-whose-cross-section-is-a-sector-of-a-cir.png)

Given that the volume of the prism is 7.65 cm³, find the possible value(s) of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
The volume of a prism is the cross-section area times the thickness. The cross-section is a sector of area $\frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $r = 2 a - 3$ and $θ = 1 . 7$

$V = \frac{1}{2} ( 2 a - 3 )^{2} ( 1 . 7 ) ( 4 ) = 7 . 65$

**[M1]**

Simplify the constant factor and divide

$3 . 4 ( 2 a - 3 )^{2} = 7 . 65$

$( 2 a - 3 )^{2} = 2 . 25$

**[A1]**

Take the square root of both sides

$2 a - 3 = \pm 1 . 5$

**[M1]**

$a = 2 . 25$* or *$a = 0 . 75$

**[A1]**

The radius $( 2 a - 3 )$ must be positive, so reject $a = 0 . 75$ (which gives $2 a - 3 = - 1 . 5$)

$a = 2 . 25$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Volume formed as $\frac{1}{2} ( 2 a - 3 )^{2} ( 1 . 7 ) ( 4 ) = 7 . 65$.
> 
> **A1**: $( 2 a - 3 )^{2} = 2 . 25$.
> 
> **M1**: Square-rooting to $2 a - 3 = \pm 1 . 5$.
> 
> **A1**: Both values $a = 2 . 25$ and $a = 0 . 75$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 2 . 25$, rejecting $a = 0 . 75$ because it gives a negative radius.

parts.problemMd:
A rainbow-shaped logo is formed from three semicircles, as shown below. Each inner semicircle has a radius that is 1 cm less than that of the next semicircle further out.

![A rainbow-shaped logo formed from three concentric semicircles sharing a centre on the flat base; the outer band between the two largest arcs is labelled A and the inner band between the two smallest arcs is labelled B; the base measures 8 cm; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/015-a-rainbow-shaped-logo-formed-from-three-concentr.png)

Find, in its simplest form, the ratio of the outer area $A$ of the logo to the inner area $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
A semicircle is a sector with angle $π$, so its area is $\frac{1}{2} π r^{2}$. The 8 cm base is the diameter of the outer semicircle, so the radii are 4 cm, 3 cm and 2 cm (each 1 cm less than the one outside it)

$\text{radii} = 4 ,  3 ,  2$

**[B1]**

Area $A$ is the band between the outer two semicircles

$A = \frac{1}{2} π ( 4 )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π ( 3 )^{2}$

**[M1]**

Area $B$ is the band between the inner two semicircles

$B = \frac{1}{2} π ( 3 )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π ( 2 )^{2}$

**[M1]**

$A = \frac{7π}{2} ,  B = \frac{5π}{2}$

**[A1]**

Write the ratio and cancel the common factor $\frac{π}{2}$

$A : B = 7 : 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct radii 4, 3 and 2 cm (outer = half the 8 cm base, each inner 1 cm less).
> 
> **M1**: Area $A$ as the difference of the outer two semicircles, $\frac{1}{2} π ( 4 )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π ( 3 )^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Area $B$ as the difference of the inner two semicircles, $\frac{1}{2} π ( 3 )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π ( 2 )^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $A = \frac{7π}{2}$ and $B = \frac{5π}{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $A : B = 7 : 5$ in simplest form.

parts.problemMd:
An eccentric wizard has captured a unicorn and will only set it free if you can answer the following question:

"I wish to create a rainbow-shaped mosaic for the floor of the throne room in my castle. The mosaic is to be formed from four semicircles, as shown below. The innermost semicircle has radius $R$ metres, and each outer semicircle has a radius that is a constant $k$ metres greater than the one immediately inside it. The rainbow mosaic must be exactly 22 metres across.

![A rainbow-shaped mosaic formed from four concentric semicircles sharing a centre on the flat base; the innermost band is labelled A, the innermost radius is labelled R m, and the base measures 22 m; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/008-a-rainbow-shaped-mosaic-formed-from-four-concent.png)

I also wish the inner region (labelled $A$ in the diagram) to take up exactly one quarter of the total area of the rainbow."

Find the required values of $R$ and $k$, and set the unicorn free.
parts.solutionMd:
A semicircle is a sector with angle $π$, so its area is $\frac{1}{2} π r^{2}$. The four radii are $R$, $R + k$, $R + 2 k$ and $R + 3 k$. The whole rainbow is the outer semicircle with the innermost part removed

$\text{Total area} = \frac{1}{2} π ( R + 3 k )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π R^{2}$

**[M1]**

The inner region $A$ is the band between the two innermost semicircles

$A = \frac{1}{2} π ( R + k )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π R^{2}$

**[M1]**

Set $A$ equal to one quarter of the total area

$\frac{\frac{1}{2}π(R+k)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}πR^{2}}{\frac{1}{2}π(R+3k)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}πR^{2}} = \frac{1}{4}$

**[M1]**

Cancel $\frac{1}{2} π$ and expand; the $R^{2}$ terms cancel, leaving $\frac{2R+k}{6R+9k} = \frac{1}{4}$. Cross-multiplying

$4 ( 2 R + k ) = 6 R + 9 k$

$2 R = 5 k$

**[A1]**

The mosaic is 22 m across, which is the diameter of the outer semicircle

$2 ( R + 3 k ) = 22$

$R + 3 k = 11$

**[M1]**

Substitute $R = \frac{5k}{2}$ into this equation

$\frac{5k}{2} + 3 k = 11$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $R = 5 \text{m}$** and **$k = 2 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Total rainbow area as $\frac{1}{2} π ( R + 3 k )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π R^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Inner region $A = \frac{1}{2} π ( R + k )^{2} - \frac{1}{2} π R^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Setting $A = \frac{1}{4} \times$ total area.
> 
> **A1**: Simplified to $2 R = 5 k$.

parts.problemMd:
A sector of a circle $O S T$ has radius $r$ cm, and the angle at the centre $O$ is $θ$ radians. The chord $S T$ has length $a$ cm.

![Sector OST of a circle, centre O at the bottom vertex; radii OS and OT each r cm, angle SOT = theta radians, and the chord ST of length a cm drawn across the top; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/010-sector-ost-of-a-circle-centre-o-at-the-bottom-ve.png)

Show that $a^{2} = 2 r^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ )$.
parts.solutionMd:
Apply the cosine rule to triangle $O S T$, which has two sides of length $r$ enclosing the angle $θ$

$a^{2} = r^{2} + r^{2} - 2 ( r ) ( r )  \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Collect the $r^{2}$ terms and factor

**Final answer:** $a^{2} = 2 r^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ )$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Cosine rule on triangle $O S T$: $a^{2} = r^{2} + r^{2} - 2 r^{2}  \text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Simplified to the printed $a^{2} = 2 r^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ )$.

parts.problemMd: Given that $r = 4 θ$ and the area of the sector is $\frac{8π^{3}}{27}$ cm², find the value of $a$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Sector OST of a circle, centre O at the bottom vertex; radii OS and OT each r cm, angle SOT = theta radians, and the chord ST of length a cm drawn across the top; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/010-sector-ost-of-a-circle-centre-o-at-the-bottom-ve.png)

First find $θ$ from the sector area, using $A = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ$ with $r = 4 θ$

$\frac{1}{2} ( 4 θ )^{2} θ = \frac{8π^{3}}{27}$

$8 θ^{3} = \frac{8π^{3}}{27}$

**[M1]**

$θ^{3} = \frac{π^{3}}{27}$

$θ = \frac{π}{3}$

**[A1]**

Now use part (a) with $r = 4 θ$, so that $r^{2} = 16 θ^{2}$

$a^{2} = 2 ( 4 θ )^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ ) = 32 θ^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ )$

**[M1]**

Substitute $θ = \frac{π}{3}$, with $\text{cos} \frac{π}{3} = \frac{1}{2}$

`a^2 = 32\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)^2\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{16\pi^2}{9}`

**[A1]**

Take the positive root, since $a$ is a chord length

$a = \frac{4π}{3} \text{cm}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Sector area $\frac{1}{2} ( 4 θ )^{2} θ = \frac{8π^{3}}{27}$, simplified to $8 θ^{3} = \frac{8π^{3}}{27}$.
> 
> **A1**: $θ = \frac{π}{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting $r = 4 θ$ into part (a): $a^{2} = 32 θ^{2} ( 1 - \text{cos}  θ )$.
> 
> **A1**: $a^{2} = \frac{16π^{2}}{9}$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = \frac{4π}{3}$ cm, rejecting the negative root since $a$ is a length.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a sector of a circle with centre $O$. The radii $O A$ and $O B$ are each $r$ cm, and the angle at the centre $A O B$ is $θ$ radians. The point $D$ lies on $O A$ and the point $C$ lies on $O B$, with $D C$ perpendicular to $O B$.

![Sector OAB of a circle, centre O at the right vertex, angle AOB = theta radians; A top-left and B bottom-left on the arc; radii OA and OB each r cm; D on OA and C on OB with DC drawn perpendicular to OB (right angle at C); the region ABCD is shaded; not to scale](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/circular-measure-radians/assets/007-sector-oab-of-a-circle-centre-o-at-the-right-ver.png)

Given that $B C : C O = 2 : 3$, show that the area of the shaded shape $A B C D$ is $\frac{1}{50} r^{2} ( 25 θ - 9  \text{tan}  θ )$ cm².
parts.solutionMd:
Since $B C : C O = 2 : 3$ and $B C + C O = O B = r$, the point $C$ divides $O B$ so that $O C$ is $\frac{3}{5}$ of the radius

$O C = \frac{3}{5} r$

**[B1]**

$D C$ is perpendicular to $O B$, so triangle $O C D$ is right-angled at $C$ with the angle $θ$ at $O$. Hence $D C = O C  \text{tan}  θ$

$D C = \frac{3}{5} r  \text{tan}  θ$

**[M1]**

The area of the right-angled triangle $O C D$ is $\frac{1}{2} \times O C \times D C$

`\text{Area }OCD = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}r\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{5}r\,\text{tan}\,\theta\right)`

**[M1]**

$= \frac{9}{50} r^{2}  \text{tan}  θ$

**[A1]**

The shaded shape $A B C D$ is the sector $O A B$ with the triangle $O C D$ removed

$A B C D = \frac{1}{2} r^{2} θ - \frac{9}{50} r^{2}  \text{tan}  θ$

**[M1]**

Factor out $\frac{1}{50} r^{2}$ (noting $\frac{1}{2} = \frac{25}{50}$)

**Final answer:** $= \frac{1}{50} r^{2} ( 25 θ - 9  \text{tan}  θ ) \text{cm}^{2}$** as required**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $O C = \frac{3}{5} r$ (from $B C : C O = 2 : 3$ with $O B = r$).
> 
> **M1**: Using the right angle at $C$ to write $D C = O C  \text{tan}  θ$.
> 
> **M1**: Triangle $O C D$ area as $\frac{1}{2} \times O C \times D C$.
> 
> **A1**: Triangle $O C D = \frac{9}{50} r^{2}  \text{tan}  θ$.
> 
> **M1**: Shaded $A B C D$ formed as sector $O A B -$ triangle $O C D$.
> 
> **A1**: Factorised to the printed $\frac{1}{50} r^{2} ( 25 θ - 9  \text{tan}  θ )$.

parts.problemMd:
The length, $l$ cm, of a spring at time $t$ seconds is modelled by

$l = 8 + 2 \text{sin}  t ,  t \geq 0 ,$

where $t$ is in radians.

State

(i) the natural length of the spring,

(ii) the maximum length of the spring,

(iii) the minimum length of the spring.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The natural (unstretched) length is the value about which the spring oscillates — the constant term, since $2 \text{sin}  t$ swings symmetrically between $- 2$ and $2$

$8 \text{cm}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The maximum length occurs when $\text{sin}  t$ takes its greatest value, $1$, giving $8 + 2$

$10 \text{cm}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The minimum length occurs when $\text{sin}  t$ takes its least value, $- 1$, giving $8 - 2$

$6 \text{cm}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: You state the natural length as 8 cm — the constant term, about which the spring oscillates.
> 
> **B1**: You state the maximum length as 10 cm.
> 
> **B1**: You state the minimum length as 6 cm.

parts.problemMd:

(ii) Find the smallest value of $t$ for which the length of the spring is 9.5 cm.

Give your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the length at this time, substitute $t = 5$ into the model, working in radians

$l = 8 + 2 \text{sin}  5$

**[M1]**

$l = 8 + 2 \times ( - 0 . 95892 \dots ) = 6 . 08215 \dots$

**Final answer:** $l = 6 . 08 \text{cm}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

To find when the spring reaches 9.5 cm, set the model equal to 9.5 and solve for $t$

$8 + 2 \text{sin}  t = 9 . 5$

**[M1]**

$\text{sin}  t = 0 . 75$

**[A1]**

The inverse sine returns the principal value, which is the first (smallest) positive solution here

$t = \text{sin}^{-1} ( 0 . 75 ) = 0 . 84806 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 0 . 848 \text{s}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: You substitute $t = 5$ into the model, working in radians. Working in degrees (which gives $l = 8 . 17$) does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct length, giving answers which round to 6.08 cm.
> 
> **M1**: You set the model equal to 9.5 and rearrange toward $\text{sin}  t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $\text{sin}  t = 0 . 75$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct smallest positive solution, giving answers which round to $t = 0 . 848$ s.

parts.problemMd: Explain why, according to this model, the spring never comes to rest.
parts.solutionMd:
The spring is at rest only if its length stops changing, so consider whether $l$ can ever settle to a constant value

**Final answer:** **Since the sine term is periodic and never decays, the length keeps oscillating between 6 cm and 10 cm and never settles to a single value**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: You explain that $\text{sin}  t$ keeps oscillating between $- 1$ and $1$ for all $t$ (it is periodic and does not decay), so the length never settles to a constant value and the spring keeps moving. Accept any equivalent explanation that the constant amplitude means the motion never dies away.

parts.problemMd:
A dolphin dives in and out of the sea. Its height, $h$ cm, relative to sea level $( h = 0 )$, at time $t$ seconds, is modelled by

$h = A \text{sin} ( B t ) ,  t \geq 0 ,$

where $A$ and $B$ are positive constants and $t$ is in radians.

On each jump and dive, the dolphin reaches a maximum height of 70 cm above sea level and a maximum depth of 70 cm below sea level.

State the value of $A$.
parts.solutionMd:
Since $\text{sin} ( B t )$ only ranges between $- 1$ and $1$, the constant $A$ is the amplitude — the greatest height (and depth) the model reaches

$A = 70$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: You state $A = 70$, recognising it as the amplitude — the maximum height of 70 cm above (and depth below) sea level. No working is needed for this "state" mark.

parts.problemMd:

Find the value of $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
One complete cycle of the motion is one full period of the sine model, so set the period equal to $π$

$\frac{2π}{B} = π$

$B = \frac{2π}{π}$

parts.problemMd:
The path of a swing boat fairground ride, which swings forwards and backwards, is modelled as the arc of a circle of radius 10 m with centre $( 0 , 12 )$, as shown in the diagram.

![Diagram of the swing boat's arc path from x = −8 to x = 8, dipping to its lowest point on the y-axis and rising to each end, with the x-axis representing ground level](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-pure-1/trigonometry/modelling-with-trigonometric-functions/assets/003-diagram-of-the-swing-boat-s-arc-path-from-x-8-to.png)

Ground level is represented by the $x$-axis. The horizontal displacement of the swing boat from the origin $O$ is $x$ metres, and its height above ground level is $y$ metres. The height of the boat is modelled by

$y = 12 - \sqrt{100-x^{2}} ,  - 8 \leq x \leq 8 .$

(i) Find the height of the boat when its horizontal displacement from the origin is 6 m.

(ii) Find the horizontal distance of the boat from the origin when it is 5 m above the ground, giving your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

(iii) Find the maximum height above the ground reached by the swing boat.

(iv) When the swing boat is at its maximum height with a positive horizontal displacement, find the angle of elevation of the boat from the origin. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the height, substitute the horizontal displacement $x = 6$ into the model

$y = 12 - \sqrt{100-6^{2}} = 12 - \sqrt{64}$

$y = 4 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

To find the horizontal distance, set the height $y = 5$ and solve for $x$

$5 = 12 - \sqrt{100-x^{2}}$

$\sqrt{100-x^{2}} = 7$

$100 - x^{2} = 49 \Rightarrow x^{2} = 51$

**[M1]**

A distance is required, so take the positive root

**Final answer:** $x = \sqrt{51} = 7 . 14 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(iii)

The height is greatest when $\sqrt{100-x^{2}}$ is smallest, which is at the ends of the swing, where $x = \pm 8$

$y = 12 - \sqrt{100-8^{2}} = 12 - \sqrt{36}$

$y = 6 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(iv)

At its maximum height the boat is at the point $( 8 , 6 )$, so the angle of elevation $θ$ from the origin satisfies

$\text{tan}  θ = \frac{6}{8}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $θ = 36 . 9 ^{\circ}$** (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct height of 4 m, from substituting $x = 6$ into the model.
> 
> **M1**: You set $y = 5$, isolate the square root and square both sides, reaching $x^{2} = 51$ (or $x = \pm \sqrt{51}$).
> 
> **A1**: Correct horizontal distance, giving answers which round to 7.14 m. As a distance is asked for, the positive root is taken.
> 
> **B1**: Correct maximum height of 6 m, recognising it occurs at the ends of the swing where $x = \pm 8$.
> 
> **M1**: You use the maximum-height point $( 8 , 6 )$ to form the correct trigonometric ratio, $\text{tan}  θ = \frac{6}{8}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct angle of elevation, giving answers which round to $36 . 9 ^{\circ}$ (accept $0 . 643$ radians).

parts.problemMd:
A Ferris wheel is modelled as a circle with centre $O ( 0 , 0 )$ and radius 100 m. There are 32 passenger pods evenly spaced around the wheel.

A pod's position is determined by the angle $θ$ radians, measured anticlockwise from the positive $x$-direction, as shown in the diagram. The coordinates $( x , y )$ of a pod are given by

$( x , y ) = ( 100 \text{cos}  θ ,  100 \text{sin}  θ ) .$

One pod is located at the point $( 100 , 0 )$, where $θ = 0$.

(i) Find the angle, in radians, between adjacent pods.

(ii) Find the coordinates, correct to 1 decimal place, of the next pod anticlockwise from $( 100 , 0 )$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The 32 pods are evenly spaced around a full turn of $2 π$ radians, so divide the full turn by the number of pods

$\frac{2π}{32} = \frac{π}{16} \text{radians}$

**[B1]**

The next pod anticlockwise is at $θ = \frac{π}{16}$, so substitute this into the coordinate model

`(x, y) = \left(100\text{cos} \; \dfrac{\pi}{16}, \; 100\text{sin} \; \dfrac{\pi}{16}\right)`

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $( 98 . 1 ,  19 . 5 )$** (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **M1**: You substitute $θ = \frac{π}{16}$ into $( 100 \text{cos}  θ ,  100 \text{sin}  θ )$, working in radians.
> 
> **A1**: Correct coordinates, giving answers which round to $( 98 . 1 ,  19 . 5 )$.
